articles.title: Major CBAM Shake-Up: EU Reportedly Plans To Exempt UK Imports From January 2026 - Carbon Herald
articles.summary: Major CBAM Shake-Up: EU Reportedly Plans To Exempt UK Imports From January 2026  Carbon Herald
articles.full_text:
- A leaked draft EU-UK summit declaration reportedly proposes exempting British goods from the EU CBAM, retroactively from January 1, 2026.
- The proposal is linked to an agreement to connect the EU ETS and UK ETS, potentially removing carbon-related trade costs between the two markets.
- The exemption remains unconfirmed and would require the necessary legal steps before companies could rely on it.
The European Union could be preparing a significant change to its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (EU CBAM), with British goods potentially receiving an exemption dating back to January 1, 2026.
A draft declaration reportedly points to progress on linking the UK ETS and EU ETS, a development that could reshape carbon-related trade between the two economies. However, the proposed CBAM exemption has not yet become law.
The development was first reported by Rapporteur, which obtained access to a draft declaration prepared ahead of the November 20 EU-UK summit in Brussels. The document reportedly indicates that linking the two carbon markets could allow British goods to avoid the EU’s carbon levy, including retrospectively from the beginning of 2026.
ETS Linkage Could Change Cross-Channel Trade
The proposed arrangement builds on commitments made during the May 2025 EU-UK summit. In its Common Understanding, both parties agreed to pursue a formal link between their respective emissions trading systems, with the intention of enabling mutual exemptions from their CBAM regimes.
The European Council subsequently authorised negotiations on ETS linkage in November 2025, explicitly identifying reciprocal CBAM exemptions as a potential benefit. The UK government has also confirmed that negotiations are underway.
For businesses, the implications could be substantial. EU importers purchasing British steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers and other covered products could potentially avoid CBAM obligations on qualifying UK-origin goods. British manufacturers would also benefit from reduced administrative requirements and potentially improved access to European customers.
Legal Questions Remain Over Retroactive Exemption
Despite the reported progress, the proposal would require changes to EU legislation, subject to approval by both the European Parliament and the Council.
Article 2(6) of the EU CBAM Regulation requires a fully linked emissions trading system agreement and an effective carbon price for a third country to qualify for exemption. The relevant country must also be included in Annex III.
The proposed January 2026 starting date raises further questions because the EU’s definitive CBAM regime only began operating on that date. The legal mechanism for applying an exemption retrospectively has not been publicly established.
Reciprocal Benefits And The Road Ahead
The UK is preparing its own CBAM for January 2027. Its Finance Act 2026 provides powers to exclude goods originating in jurisdictions with linked emissions trading systems, creating a potential route to reciprocal treatment for EU exporters.
The November 20 summit could provide further political clarity, although Reuters and the Financial Times have reported that some elements of the broader EU-UK package may require additional negotiations after the meeting.
Until the linking agreement is concluded and the necessary legislation takes effect, companies should continue following existing reporting and compliance requirements. Nevertheless, the reported proposal signals a potentially important acceleration in EU-UK carbon-market integration, with consequences extending well beyond the CBAM itself.

articles.summary: European Commission confirms Ukraine meets conditions to open all EU accession negotiating clusters – PM  Interfax-Ukraine

Facts
European Commission confirms Ukraine meets conditions to open all EU accession negotiating clusters – PM
The European Commission has confirmed that Ukraine has met the conditions for opening all remaining negotiating clusters in its EU accession process, while its progress in preparing for membership has improved in nine chapters, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said.
"Today, the European Commission's report was personally handed to me by EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarina Mathernova. The European Commission confirmed that Ukraine has met the conditions for opening all remaining clusters. The state of preparation for accession has improved in nine chapters. This is more than twice as many as last year. There has been no deterioration in any chapter, nor any rollback of reforms," Koretsky wrote on Telegram on Wednesday.
He said the European Commission had noted good or very good progress in 10 chapters, including energy, the digital sector, financial services, taxation, education, science, agriculture and customs.
He also said that, for the first time, foreign policy, security and defense had received the highest progress assessment. The European Commission also noted the independent and effective work of Ukraine's anti-corruption institutions, as well as improved assessments in the areas of the judiciary and justice.
"The next goal is to receive an Interim Benchmark Assessment Report (IBAR) in early 2027. To this end, at the initiative of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a joint Ukraine-EU working group has been established. We are setting ambitious but achievable goals. There are areas where we need to work faster. We are taking the European Commission's recommendations forward," Koretsky said.

India and the EU are expected to sign the FTA by mid-December. articles.title: Midterms 2026 : après la déroute républicaine, l’Ukraine nourrit le maigre espoir de freiner la dérive américaine en faveur de la Russie
articles.summary: En exigeant de la Maison Blanche davantage de transparence sur ses projets d’affaires avec Moscou et en déclenchant des commissions d’enquête sur la politique de soutien à Kiev, la majorité démocrate au Congrès pourrait rééquilibrer la position de Washington.
articles.full_text:
Quarante-huit heures à peine après la déroute électorale de Donald Trump, mardi 3 novembre, lors des élections américaines de mi-mandat, Kirill Dmitriev, l’homme lige de Vladimir Poutine, était attendu à Washington. Comme pour témoigner d’une bienveillance russe intacte à l’égard du président américain, ce dirigeant de fonds d’investissement devait être reçu, jeudi, par la première dame, Melania Trump. Officiellement, le Russe doit évoquer avec des représentants de l’Ukraine les enjeux humanitaires de la mission menée par l’épouse de Donald Trump après l’évacuation des résidents martyrs de la ville ukrainienne d’Olechky, assiégée durant de long mois.
Mais à Washington, M. Dimitriev, architecte des projets de « deals » énergétiques et financiers russo-américains qui font saliver l’administration Trump, travaillera surtout, en coulisse, à la levée des sanctions américaines visant son fonds, le RIDF, autrefois qualifié par les Etats-Unis de caisse noire du Kremlin. La Russie espère que l’écrasante victoire des démocrates, qui ont emporté la majorité des sièges au Sénat et à la Chambre des représentants, n’est pas de nature à modifier l’attitude du milliardaire, pressé de faire affaire avec Moscou, en passant par pertes et profits le sort de l’Ukraine. La Maison Blanche n’a-t-elle pas rappelé aux Américains cette évidence, mercredi sur X, au sortir du scrutin : « Trump est toujours votre président ! »
Promis à une seconde moitié de mandat de « lame duck » (canard boiteux), privé de majorité au Congrès, Donald Trump est « gravement affaibli politiquement, en perte d’influence et vulnérable », juge Stephen Sestanovich, expert au Council on Foreign Relations et ancien ambassadeur itinérant du département d’Etat pour l’ex-Union soviétique, estimant que les Européens, s’ils manœuvrent habilement, pourraient rétablir un semblant de soutien américain à l’égard de l’Ukraine, ou du moins freiner la dérive en cours.
Après l’annonce, début octobre, d’un « deal » pour acheter à la Russie du diesel, malgré les sanctions américaines contre le pays, puis la menace de stopper la fourniture du renseignement américain à Kiev et l’interruption du réseau internet Starlink du milliardaire trumpiste Elon Musk, crucial pour la ligne de front, le président ukrainien, Volodymyr Zelensky s’était ému d’une « trahison » des Etats-Unis.

articles.summary: Alors que les mouvements de jeunes ont demandé un relais du monde du travail, les organisations syndicales ont appelé à défiler et à cesser le travail, jeudi, dans toute la France. articles.full_text:
La date a été fixée longtemps à l’avance. Le 5 octobre, soit six jours après une journée d’action dans la fonction publique et alors que la contestation lycéenne prenait son envol, cinq syndicats de salariés (CFDT, CGT, FO, FSU, UNSA) ont appelé à défiler et à cesser le travail, jeudi 5 novembre. Leurs mots d’ordre sont larges : revalorisation du smic, ouverture « immédiate » de négociations sur les rémunérations, sauvegarde des services publics, de l’emploi et de l’industrie, justice fiscale par la taxation des gros patrimoines…
Depuis, la fronde dans l’enseignement secondaire s’est élargie aux universités et a connu une ampleur historique, se muant en un mouvement social qui embarque de multiples catégories : élèves, étudiants, travailleurs du privé et du public, anciens et nouveaux « gilets jaunes », parents et citoyens choqués par la brutalité des interventions policières à l’encontre des lycéens, notamment.
Après les trois « actes » des 17, 24 et 31 octobre contre – entre autres revendications – la vie chère, le rendez-vous de jeudi change de dimension : « Ça doit être une grande journée de convergence », a martelé, le 2 novembre, Sophie Binet, la secrétaire générale de la CGT, sur France 2. Fatigués par plus d’un mois de luttes, des lycéens le répètent : ils ont « besoin du relais » « du monde du travail ». Depuis que l’appel à manifester et à faire grève a été diffusé, trois autres organisations ont décidé de s’y associer : la CFTC, Solidaires et la CFE-CGC.

articles.title: EU AI Act transparency rules show why businesses can’t afford to wait - IT Security Guru
articles.summary: EU AI Act transparency rules show why businesses can’t afford to wait  IT Security Guru
articles.full_text:
By Khush Kashyap, Senior Director of Governance, Risk and Compliance at Vanta
Transparency goes hand in hand with AI. Or at least it’s meant to.
Until now, transparency has mostly depended on how forthcoming people are about using AI. Detection tools can’t carry that weight on their own.
That is now changing. The EU AI Act’s transparency requirements, which came into effect this August, call on providers and deployers of certain AI systems to label or disclose content that is generated or manipulated by AI. Now, providers such as Anthropic and OpenAI have started to act.
This reflects a broader shift in AI regulation: transparency and traceability are moving from principles to practical requirements.
But, for businesses, the picture is far from clear. First, as regulators attempt to establish workable standards for identifying AI-generated content, the technology itself continues to evolve, making it a moving target. Second, while parts of the EU AI Act’s regulatory framework are moving forward, others, such as high-risk AI obligations are being pushed back.
This leaves businesses with a clear choice: wait for every detail to be settled, or start building the visibility and accountability that meaningful transparency requires.
Watermarking is only the tip of the AI governance iceberg
Watermarking is seen by many to reflect the EU AI Act requirements. But businesses must consider the limitations of the technology and whether it can provide reliable, lasting proof that content was generated or manipulated by AI.
A text watermark doesn’t survive much. Paraphrase it, translate it, or run it through a model that doesn’t watermark, and it’s gone. OpenAI’s own approach to EU text provenance rules makes the point with numbers: replacing a quarter of the words with synonyms dropped detection from roughly 92% to 17%, and shorter passages are far harder to detect in the first place.
The debate around watermarking tells us a lot about the practical challenges of regulating AI. This approach may help demonstrate transparency, but it cannot explain how AI is being used, whether human oversight took place or who is accountable for the outcome.
Look at how differently two providers have answered the same rule: Anthropic watermarks everywhere, while OpenAI turns it on by default only in the EU. If the technical layer is this unsettled, your governance can’t depend on it.
For this, broader AI governance is what’s needed.
The wider context of the EU AI Act
These implications extend far beyond watermarking.The Digital Omnibus, a separate amending regulation finalised in July, has pushed the high-risk deadlines out — to December 2027 for Annex III systems and August 2028 for AI in regulated products — and has also changed some of the Act’s definitions.
For instance, the definition of a “safety component” has been narrowed, so systems used purely for user assistance, performance optimisation, automation or convenience no longer automatically qualify — though the carve-out falls away the moment a failure could endanger health or safety.
These changes may affect which systems fall into the highest-risk categories, but requirements and prohibitions demonstrate that the regulatory direction of travel remains towards greater accountability, transparency and evidence.
My advice is simple: don’t set your pace by regulatory deadlines. If you wait for every standard to be finalised before you act, you end up doing it all in a rush — and that’s how you get security theatre, where more time goes into proving security than improving it.
The combination of new transparency requirements and extended timelines gives businesses two things they rarely have: clarity about the direction of travel, and more time. They should therefore treat it as a rare opportunity to build meaningful governance infrastructure before they are forced to do so.
Three priorities organisations should tackle now
Action doesn’t always equal governance. If organisations focus on producing labels or paperwork without understanding how AI is being used in practice, they are still exposing themselves to the same risks. They may understand whether their organisation uses AI, but not where it appears across products, workflows and customer interactions.
The following priorities can help businesses build the foundations they will need as future obligations take effect.
Build a complete AI asset inventory
Everything starts with visibility. Begin by identifying every AI system across your organisation, including tools introduced informally by teams or embedded within existing products and across your network.
Then understand what each system does, the data it processes, who owns it and its likely risk classification under the EU AI Act. This can help you understand where controls and evidence are still missing, and where risk is likely to grow.
Conduct AI impact assessments
For higher-risk AI systems, establish documented evaluations before deployment and when your systems change.
Assess factors such as bias, human oversight, transparency, accountability, security and data handling in a structured way. These assessments can serve a similar practical purpose to GDPR’s DPIAs by recording the risks identified, the controls applied and the decisions made.
The Act has its own fundamental rights impact assessments for certain deployers, but those sit in the delayed high-risk package — another reason to build the muscle now.
Create clear AI governance structures
Develop practical AI policies that cover acceptable use, data handling, human review and third-party AI tools. As part of this, assign clear ownership for AI governance across your organisation’s security, privacy, legal, compliance and product teams.
Be sure to maintain audit trails that show how systems were approved, what controls were applied and how risks are monitored over time. Governance should be proportionate to risk and scale as regulation evolves. This is how it supports responsible innovation, instead of slowing it down.
Turning transparency into action
Whatever side you take, the watermarking debate tells us that AI regulation is becoming increasingly tangible.
But we must avoid interpreting delays in the EU AI Act as reduced regulatory ambition or a free pass from responsibility. Instead, it must be treated as additional preparation time. Organisations that spend this time building robust AI governance programmes that give them the confidence to understand how AI works, the evidence to show how it is governed and the means to build better, more trusted products.
Right now, we are focused on whether AI-generated content can be identified. Instead, we need to ask ourselves if we can explain where AI is being used, what risks it creates and what controls are in place to manage it. So that transparency goes beyond the checkbox and becomes an ongoing capability.

articles.title: The EU AI Act has entered the real world: What organizations need to do now - SC Media
articles.summary: The EU AI Act has entered the real world: What organizations need to do now  SC Media
articles.full_text:
COMMENTARY: The EU AI Act entered into force on Aug. 1, 2024. Two years later, on Aug. 2, 2026, its broader application phase began, with several obligations already active and others scheduled for later stages.
More importantly, the European Commission’s AI Office and national competent authorities now have enforcement powers for provisions applicable at this stage.
[SC Media Perspectives columns are written by a trusted community of SC Media cybersecurity subject matter experts. Read more Perspectives here.]
This changes the conversation.
AI governance can no longer be treated simply as a future compliance project.
What has changed?
The EU’s prohibited AI practices and AI literacy requirements have applied since Feb. 2, 2025. Governance requirements and obligations for general-purpose AI models followed on Aug. 2, 2025.
On Aug. 2, 2026, enforcement expanded alongside further transparency requirements.
Article 50 introduces transparency obligations for certain AI interactions and AI-generated or manipulated content. Depending on the use case, people may need to know when they are interacting with AI, while certain synthetic content must be identifiable.
There is also a limited transition for certain marking and detection requirements: systems placed on the market before Aug. 2, 2026, have until Dec. 2, 2026, for the relevant obligations.
This matters because 2026 is not one single compliance deadline.
The AI Act is a phased program.
The next deadlines matter
The next major milestone is Dec. 2, 2026, followed by the scheduled application of rules for certain high-risk AI systems on Dec. 2, 2027. AI systems embedded in regulated products have a later date of Aug. 2, 2028.
That additional time should not be interpreted as permission to wait.
High-risk AI governance can involve risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record keeping, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity.
Building these capabilities across a complex organization takes time.
The financial exposure is significant
The AI Act establishes substantial maximum penalties.
For prohibited AI practices and certain data-related infringements, fines can reach €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.
For other breaches, the maximum can reach €15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover. Providing incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities can result in penalties of up to €7.5 million or 1% of worldwide annual turnover, subject to the regulation’s applicable rules and proportionality provisions.
These numbers change the level at which AI governance should be discussed.
This is no longer only an IT issue. It is an enterprise risk and board-level governance issue.
The biggest weakness may be visibility
One of the first questions I would ask an organization is simple: “Show me your AI inventory.”
Many organizations have mature IT asset inventories but still cannot confidently answer that question.
AI can enter through enterprise applications, cloud services, recruitment platforms, development tools, security products, marketing systems and employee experimentation.
This creates "shadow AI" — technology being used without sufficient organisational visibility or assessment.
A meaningful AI inventory should identify the system, provider, business purpose, owner, data processed, affected users, AI role and risk classification.
Without that visibility, compliance becomes difficult to demonstrate.
AI governance must connect with cybersecurity
The AI Act should not become another isolated compliance program.
AI governance should connect with ISO/IEC 27001, privacy, cybersecurity, supplier risk, procurement, enterprise risk management and internal audit.
Consider a simple example: an employee uploads confidential company information into an external AI service. That is not simply an AI issue. It can involve information classification, data protection, supplier risk, access control and employee awareness.
AI crosses traditional governance boundaries.
What should organizations do now?
1. Build an AI inventory. Identify approved and unauthorised AI use.
2. Classify the use cases. Determine which requirements apply.
3. Assign ownership. Establish clear accountability for material AI systems.
4. Review suppliers. Do not assume purchasing an AI-enabled product transfers all compliance responsibility to the vendor.
5. Integrate AI into risk management. Assess AI alongside cybersecurity, privacy, operational and supplier risks.
6. Establish evidence. Maintain assessments, approvals, training records, supplier reviews, technical documentation, monitoring and corrective actions.
7. Prepare for the next deadlines. Address upcoming requirements now rather than waiting for the deadline.
The auditor’s question
The most important question may not be: “Do we have an AI policy?”
It should be: “Can we demonstrate that we know what AI we use, understand its risks, know who is accountable, have implemented appropriate controls and can produce evidence when challenged?”
That is the real shift.
The organizations that respond well will not simply produce more documentation. They will make AI governance part of normal business control.
- Know your AI.
- Understand its risk.
- Assign accountability.
- Control it.
- Keep the evidence.
That is what AI readiness should look like as regulation moves from the rulebook into the real world.

articles.title: EU AI Act Timeline: 5 Dates to 2028 [2026] - shattered.io
articles.summary: EU AI Act Timeline: 5 Dates to 2028 [2026]  shattered.io
articles.full_text:
The EU AI Act, formally Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024, is now deep into its phased rollout. The European Commission’s AI Act Service Desk timeline lays out the sequence, and it ends with the main application milestones foreseen to be completed by 2 August 2028. As of today, November 04, 2026, the first three waves of rules are already live, and two more are scheduled.
That matters well beyond Brussels. Any team that builds, fine-tunes, hosts or deploys AI for users in the European Union has to map its products against a calendar that started in February 2025. Engineers who already run content filters and policy layers, for example the kind we walked through in our 12-step AI guardrails tutorial, will find that several legal duties line up with controls they ship anyway.
This analysis walks through what the law says, which dates are fixed, what the Commission has published about enforcement, and what builders should plan for. It sticks to the verified timeline and to material from official EU channels. Where we offer judgment, we label it as our analysis. Where the record is silent, such as fine amounts or named company cases, we say so rather than guess.
What the EU AI Act Is and Why It Matters
The regulation sets harmonised rules for artificial-intelligence systems across the European Union. Its stated purpose, per the Commission, is to protect health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, the rule of law and the environment while keeping the single market open to AI products. The text entered into force on 1 August 2024, which makes it the first binding horizontal law on AI from a major jurisdiction.
The word “horizontal” carries weight here. The Act does not regulate one industry. It regulates AI by function and risk, so a chatbot on a retail site, a text generator inside an office suite and a foundation model sold through an API all land inside its scope. Obligations differ by role. A provider that places a system on the EU market carries different duties from a deployer that uses someone else’s system.
For readers in the United States and elsewhere, the reach question comes first. The Commission’s own pages describe obligations tied to the EU market, not to where a company is headquartered. A US startup that offers a model or an AI feature to EU users therefore has to treat the Act as a product requirement, much as the GDPR forced global privacy changes after 2018. That comparison is our framing, not a Commission statement, but it explains why compliance teams outside Europe track every milestone.
The Act also reshapes how technical teams talk to lawyers. Terms like general-purpose AI model, systemic risk, provider, deployer and synthetic content now carry defined meanings. Product managers who ignore those definitions risk misclassifying a feature, and misclassification is where most compliance mistakes begin.
The Official Timeline: Five Dates From 2025 to 2028
The Commission’s implementation timeline breaks the Act into stages rather than a single switch-on day. The table below consolidates the dates confirmed in the official sources. It separates what already applies from what is still ahead.
| Date | What applies | Status on 4 Nov 2026 | 
|---|---|---|
| 1 August 2024 | Regulation enters into force | Done | 
| 2 February 2025 | Prohibitions, definitions and AI-literacy provisions | Applying | 
| 2 August 2025 | Governance rules and obligations for general-purpose AI models | Applying | 
| 2 August 2026 | Article 50 transparency requirements and main enforcement start | Applying | 
| 2 December 2027 | Obligations for high-risk systems listed in Annex III | Scheduled | 
| 2 August 2028 | Obligations for high-risk systems embedded in regulated products (Annex I) | Scheduled | 
Source: European Commission AI Act Service Desk and implementation timeline pages. Note the pattern. The law front-loads the bans and the model-level rules, then pushes the heaviest product-conformity work out to late 2027 and 2028. That ordering gives regulators time to stand up bodies and gives industry time to finish technical standards.
February 2025: Prohibitions and AI Literacy Arrive
The first wave landed on 2 February 2025. The Commission lists three elements as applicable from that date: the prohibitions, the definitions and the AI-literacy provisions. The prohibitions put hard limits on certain AI practices inside the EU, and violations can incur fines of up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover, according to the European Commission. Because the fact sheet behind this report does not enumerate each banned practice, we will not list them here. Readers should check the regulation text or the Commission’s guidance pages for the exact scope.
The AI-literacy provisions matter more than they first appear. They push organizations to make sure the people who operate and oversee AI systems understand what those systems can and cannot do. In practice that means training, documentation and internal policy, not a software patch. Many firms treated literacy as a soft item in early 2025. By late 2026, auditors and customers increasingly ask for proof of it.
Definitions also did real work in this first wave. By fixing what counts as an AI system, a provider and a deployer, the Act settled arguments that would otherwise have lingered for years. Legal teams could finally classify products against shared terms. That sounds dry, but it is the groundwork every later duty depends on.
City and state governments elsewhere have started to regulate narrower slices of the same problem. Our earlier report on New York City’s AI hiring rule shows the contrast. The EU wrote one framework for the whole market, while US jurisdictions so far have moved use case by use case.
August 2025: General-Purpose AI Rules Switch On
The second wave, applicable from 2 August 2025, covers governance rules and obligations for general-purpose AI models. This is the part of the Act that speaks most directly to the companies building large language models and other foundation models. According to the Commission’s digital strategy pages, providers of these models must prepare technical documentation, pass information to downstream providers, put a copyright-compliance policy in place and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training. The Commission adds that breaches of these general-purpose AI rules can trigger fines of up to €15 million or 3% of global turnover.
The copyright element draws the most debate. Providers must maintain a policy for complying with EU copyright law, including any text-and-data-mining opt-outs rightsholders have declared. That requirement has pushed the industry toward machine-readable opt-out signals. We covered one such effort in our report on four AI developers backing one opt-out token, which shows how quickly the technical ecosystem moved once the legal duty existed.
Systemic-Risk Models Face Extra Duties
The Commission describes a higher tier for the most advanced general-purpose models, classed as carrying systemic risk. Providers of those models face added duties covering model evaluations, adversarial testing, systemic-risk assessment, serious-incident reporting and cybersecurity. The risk categories the Commission names include chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear misuse, cyberattacks, harmful manipulation and loss of control.
The Commission’s pages do not publish a list of named models in that tier in the material we retrieved. The classification depends on a model’s legal designation and capabilities, not on its brand or launch date. Anyone claiming a specific commercial model is or is not designated should point to an official notice.
Who Governs the Models
The official implementation timeline identifies three bodies tied to general-purpose AI governance: the AI Board, the Scientific Panel and the Advisory Forum. The European AI Office holds supervisory and enforcement responsibility for general-purpose models, according to the Service Desk, while national authorities stay central for many rules that govern AI systems.
August 2026: Article 50 Transparency and Enforcement Begin
The third wave arrived on 2 August 2026, three months ago. Two things switched on together. The Article 50 transparency requirements began to apply, and the main enforcement powers started for applicable provisions. The Service Desk states that from that date some enforcement powers of the AI Office and of Member State authorities start to apply, covering prohibited practices, transparency requirements for certain AI systems and the rules for general-purpose AI models.
Article 50 is the section most users will actually feel. Per the Commission’s Article 50 pages, providers of AI systems that interact directly with people, such as chatbots, agents and avatars, must make sure users know they are dealing with AI unless that is obvious from context. Providers of systems that generate synthetic audio, images, video or text must ensure outputs carry machine-readable markings that identify them as AI-generated or manipulated. The Commission says those markings must be effective, reliable, robust and interoperable.
The article also covers disclosure of deepfakes and certain AI-generated or manipulated content. Deployers of emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation systems must inform the people exposed to them. The Commission’s 2026 Article 50 guidelines add that the marking duty expressly reaches general-purpose AI systems when they generate synthetic audio, image, video or text.

articles.title: EU AI act: the world’s first law on artificial intelligence - Meer | English edition
articles.summary: EU AI act: the world’s first law on artificial intelligence  Meer | English edition
articles.full_text:
Artificial intelligence is transforming the way we live, work, and interact, often faster than governments or citizens can keep up. For years, this powerful technology developed in a near-legal vacuum, raising hopes of innovation but also fears of abuse. That changed when the European Union introduced the AI Act, the world’s first comprehensive law governing the use of artificial intelligence. More than a legal milestone, the Act is Europe’s declaration that technology must serve society, not the other way around. Just as the EU’s landmark data protection rules reshaped global privacy standards, this bold new framework is set to influence how AI is built and deployed far beyond Europe’s borders.
A law years in the making
Brussels has spent years wrestling with a simple but urgent question: how do you regulate a technology that changes faster than politics? The European Commission launched its proposal in 2021, setting off a long process of debate and negotiation. After intense lobbying and compromise, the European Parliament approved the final text in March 2024, and EU governments in the Council gave their backing two months later. On August 1, the AI Act officially entered into force, marking a global first.1
However, the AI Act is not being implemented all at once. Some provisions, such as bans on the most dangerous AI systems, took effect within six months. Others will be phased in over the next three years, giving companies space to adapt.2 This slow rollout reflects both the ambition of the legislation and the difficulty of writing rules for a technology that refuses to stand still.
A risk-based outlook
The core of the AI Act is its risk-based approach. Instead of treating all algorithms the same, the EU categorized AI systems. “Unacceptable risk” systems are banned completely. This includes social scoring, where people are judged by automated systems, and unauthorized real-time biometric surveillance. “High-risk” systems, such as AI used in healthcare, policing, or hiring, are allowed only under strict conditions. They must meet standards for transparency, oversight, and safety testing. “Limited risk” systems, like deepfakes, must inform users that they are interacting with AI. “Minimal risk” tools, such as spam filters, face little regulation.3
The rise of foundation models
A recent addition to the AI Act is its emphasis on general-purpose AI (GPAI). These are large, adaptable systems like ChatGPT that can write text, answer questions, or generate code. Unlike AI designed for a single task, foundation models can be built into many different products and services, from chatbots to medical tools. That versatility makes them powerful but also unpredictable, which is why the EU decided they deserve their own set of rules.
From August 2025, GPAI providers will face strict transparency obligations. They must share technical documentation with regulators and with companies that rely on their models, publish a summary of the data used for training, and adopt policies to respect copyright law. These measures are meant to lift the lid on systems that are often treated as “black boxes,” giving both officials and the public a clearer picture of how they work and what fuels them.4
For models considered a systemic risk, meaning they are so large or widely used that failures could have serious consequences, the rules go further. Developers must run safety tests, report serious incidents, and put strong cybersecurity protections in place.5 By carving out these additional safeguards, the EU is signalling that foundation models are not just another type of AI but the engines of the digital future. The aim is to make them accountable without cutting off the innovation they promise.
Who falls under the law?
The scope of the AI Act is intentionally broad. It does not just cover European tech companies but also any foreign business whose AI systems are used inside the EU. A U.S. startup offering AI-driven hiring software in Berlin, or a Chinese company selling facial-recognition tools in Paris, would both have to play by Europe’s rules. Just as the EU’s data protection law (GDPR) set the global benchmark for privacy, the AI Act is expected to export European standards around the world.6
There are, however, a few exceptions. According to Recital 24 of the AI Act, AI built for military or national security purposes is excluded, as is research still in the lab. But once an AI system makes the leap from experimentation to the marketplace, the law applies. The idea is simple: innovation should thrive in early stages, but once AI enters people’s daily lives, it must be subject to safeguards that protect society.
The watchdogs of AI
Regulating artificial intelligence is no small task, so the EU has set up new institutions to keep watch. At the centre is the European AI Office, a body within the European Commission that will monitor compliance and step in when powerful general-purpose models step out of line. National authorities in each member state will also play a role, coordinated to make sure the rules are applied consistently across the Union.
To avoid leaving these decisions to politicians and lawyers alone, the framework also brings in outside voices. An independent panel of scientists will provide technical expertise, while an advisory forum will give civil society groups and industry representatives a seat at the table. The aim is to strike a balance: rules that are rigorous enough to keep people safe, but also legitimate and inclusive enough to earn public trust.7
Power, penalties, and the politics of innovation
The AI Act comes with teeth. Companies caught using banned systems can be fined up to €35 million or seven percent of their global revenue. Even lesser violations carry fines of up to €15 million or three percent of revenue, as stipulated in Article 99 of the AI Act. These numbers are not symbolic. They echo the strict enforcement of the EU’s data protection law, GDPR, where regulators showed they were willing to take on some of the world’s biggest companies. Few expect the AI Act to be any different.
But big penalties are only part of the story. The law has also sparked debate about whether strict regulation will stifle innovation. Critics warn that compliance costs could hit startups hardest, leaving them unable to compete with large tech firms that have the resources to cope. Even some European leaders share these concerns.8 Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has called parts of the law confusing and burdensome, suggesting that the EU may be undermining its own competitiveness.9
Supporters counter that clear rules are the key to building public trust. If citizens feel protected, they argue, they will be more willing to accept AI in sensitive areas like healthcare or finance. For them, the AI Act is not an obstacle to innovation but the foundation of an ethical and sustainable digital economy.10 The clash of views reveals a familiar European challenge: how to regulate boldly without slowing growth in a global race.
From daily life to global influence
While the political debate continues, industries are already adjusting. In fashion, AI tools that recommend outfits or run virtual fitting rooms now need human oversight and transparency. In media, generative systems must be labeled or watermarked, reshaping how audiences consume images and video. Even American companies are rethinking their practices, updating documentation and audit processes to avoid trouble with European regulators. Just as GDPR became the world’s privacy benchmark, the AI Act is already pushing firms worldwide to design safer, more transparent AI.
The stakes extend far beyond Europe. In the United States, the government has issued executive orders and voluntary guidelines, but no binding law. China has drawn up its own rules, shaped by its political priorities. This patchwork approach has left the global AI landscape divided. Against this backdrop, Europe is positioning itself as the champion of trustworthy AI. Whether other powers will follow its lead remains uncertain, but the EU has already made one point clear: artificial intelligence will not remain a lawless frontier.
Conclusion: a bold experiment
The AI Act is both pioneering and imperfect. It is pioneering because Europe has chosen to write rules for artificial intelligence before the technology has fully matured. It is imperfect because no law can anticipate every risk, every breakthrough, or every misuse that may still emerge.
What matters is that Europe has acted. By putting forward the world’s first comprehensive framework, the EU hopes to protect its citizens while shaping the terms of the global debate. The gamble is clear: that democratic societies can harness technological power without sacrificing rights or trust. Whether other nations follow Europe’s lead or strike out on their own path, one thing is certain. Artificial intelligence will no longer develop in a vacuum, and the rules written in Brussels will be impossible to ignore.

2 EU Artificial Intelligence Act, “Implementation Timeline,” EU Artificial Intelligence Act, last updated 1 August 2024.
3 European Commission, “AI Act Enters into Force,” European Commission, August 1, 2024.
4 Ibid.
5 European Commission, “The General-Purpose AI Code of Practice,” European Commission, 10 July 2025.
6 European Commission, “AI Act,” European Commission, 25 July 2025.
7 Ibid.
8 Public Cloud Group, “Between Innovation and Regulation: The EU AI Act,” PCG, 28 March 2024.
9 Pieter Haeck, “Swedish PM Calls for a Pause of the EU’s AI Rules,” Politico, 23 June 2025.
10 Raluca Csernatoni, “The EU’s AI Power Play: Between Deregulation and Innovation,” Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, May 20, 2025.

articles.title: Left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins in Michigan to become first Muslim senator - BBC
articles.summary: Left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins in Michigan to become first Muslim senator  BBCPolitics of fear failed to stop El-Sayed's historic US Senate win  ReutersGiddy Democrats let the mask slip with DEI boasts and Arabic taunts  The TelegraphAbdul El-Sayed’s Senate Win Is Big to Muslim Americans, but Not Because of Faith  The New York TimesAbdul El-Sayed welcomes Trump's plan to cut Israel aid, calls for end to arms sales  NPR
articles.full_text:
Left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has won in the battleground state of Michigan to become the US's first Muslim senator, following a race fuelled by withering attacks and inter-party disputes.
El-Sayed bested Republican Mike Rogers, withstanding an onslaught of attacks that included baselessly tying him to terrorism and a high-profile spat with a fellow Democrat.
Rogers, backed by President Donald Trump, portrayed El-Sayed as a communist, criticising his stance on Israel and his Muslim faith.
After waiting long hours, watching the wave of Democratic gains across the country, El-Sayed's supporters celebrated wildly when he took the stage to mark his victory.
The former public health administrator campaigned on a left-wing platform that included universal health care and a wealth tax on billionaires.
The win comes days after El-Sayed's Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens, endorsed Rogers, the Republican candidate, just days before the election.
El-Sayed's supporters gave deafening cheers when he took to the stage, as they chanted his name in jubilation. A sea of iPhones were held up to take in this moment of history - a Muslim man elected to the Senate.
Several people in the crowd embraced, filled with emotion. They repeated his slogan back to him like they were at a concert: "Money out of politics, money in your pocket and Medicare for all."
On the campaign trail, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, described Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide and called for an end to US aid to the country.
The issue carries particular resonance in Michigan, which is home to the second largest Arab-American population in the US.
It also fuelled tensions between El-Sayed and Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, whose primary campaign received millions of dollars in backing from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac).
The contest was widely seen as a test of the political influence of the Democratic left in a key battleground state, following a series of primary wins by democratic socialist candidates in more politically favoured districts.
El-Sayed thanked the crowd in the early hours of Wednesday morning for taking a chance on "the unlikeliest of candidates" and rounded on his opponents.
"They went all in on one of the ugliest campaigns we've seen in a long time," he said, accusing them of attacking him "because of my name and my faith".
"They wanted an America that is too small for some of us. We know that this is an America that is big enough for all of us," El-Sayed added.
Supporters 'proud' of win
This is a milestone for Muslim Americans who had to watch, along with their children, as El-Sayed was attacked with increasing anti-Muslim rhetoric, including directly from the president of the United States. It comes at a time of rising in Islamophobia nationwide.
Roula Allouch, an Arab American Muslim, told the BBC she had goosebumps from the success of the campaign.
"I'm proud of Abdul, the campaign that he ran, his family for their perseverance through all the hate, the Islamophobic rhetoric that was thrown at him throughout this campaign," she said.
Another Muslim woman in the crowd was equally moved and told the BBC his win meant everything to her.
"He makes us so proud and it just makes us feel like we can stand a little taller, broaden our shoulders and know somebody has our back and that he's going to be in Washington really fighting for us," she said.
El-Sayed has certainly shown on the campaign trail that he's willing to hit back at Maga attacks. In his victory speech, he used the Arabic phrase "Alhamdullah", and then trolled Republicans by saying that "for the rightwing ops, that just means praise be to God".
El-Sayed, 42, represents a generation of Arab Americans and Muslims who were born in the United States to immigrant parents and grew up in post-9/11 America.
Celebrating with family from Chicago, another South Asian Muslim supporter of El-Sayed's said the moment was historic for everyone who has been made to feel that they don't belong in America or have a place in politics.
"If someone with the name of Abdul can make it, that means this next generation can look up and say that they can too," she told the BBC.
'One of the tightest races'
The Michigan Senate seat, previously held by retiring Democrat Gary Peters, was considered by analysts to be one of the tightest races in Tuesday's midterm elections.
El-Sayed's win further cements Democrats' control of the US Senate after a wave of wins - including in deep-Republican areas.
He had to contend with massive outside spending heavily favouring Rogers and his opponent in the Democratic primary, Haley Stevens. He's been unapologetic and unwavering in his stances.
In presidential elections, Michigan is one of the crucial swing states - the state voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but Donald Trump in 2024.
Many had questioned whether Stevens' last-minute endorsement of Rogers would make a difference in the race.
Democratic leadership called it "a despicable betrayal" and her staff reportedly resigned in mass. Voters who spoke with the BBC in the state said they were confused over the move, with some questioning whether the congresswoman was acting out of anger.
El-Sayed attempted to ignore the dramatic turn, telling reporters that he doesn't "think about Haley Stevens" and "none of this matters".
Throughout his campaign, El-Sayed has channelled grassroots frustration with Washington politics as well as US ties to Israel. He took on money in politics and argued against Trump's policies, which he blamed for raising costs for voters in the state.
He campaigned with left-wing leaders Sen Bernie Sanders and Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

articles.title: Isometric Launches New CBAM Data Preparation and Reporting Service for Exporters - ESG Today
articles.summary: Isometric Launches New CBAM Data Preparation and Reporting Service for Exporters  ESG Today
articles.full_text:
Industrial certification provider Isometric announced today the launch of Ready for CBAM, a new service aimed at helping companies exporting to the EU prepare emissions data for verification under the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), the EU’s carbon tax on imported goods.
CBAM was adopted in 2023, and entered into force at the beginning of 2026, to establish a mechanism designed to avoid “carbon leakage,” a situation in which companies move production of emissions-intensive goods to countries with less stringent environmental and climate policies. CBAM is aimed at equalizing the price of carbon paid for EU products operating under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) – the EU’s internal cap and trade carbon pricing mechanism – with that paid for products produced in other countries, with companies that import into the EU required to purchase CBAM certificates in order to make up the difference.
Under CBAM, EU importers are required to purchase certificates covering the emissions embedded in imported goods, calculated using either actual emissions data verified by an accredited verifier or default values established by the EU. For most covered goods, the default values include a markup that increases from 10% in 2026 to 30% by 2028, potentially increasing costs for importers without verified emissions data.
EU importers are required to submit their first CBAM declarations, covering 2026 imports, by September 30, 2027. Errors in submissions may require additional rounds of review, Isometric said.
Under the new service, Isometric said that its carbon accounting experts work with exporters to prepare the monitoring plan and emissions report for each plant, with its AI-powered platform checking the data as it is uploaded and flagging any issues, while the experts then review the full submission against the EU’s rules. The service continues through the verification process, with the experts working with the exporter to resolve issues raised by the verifier, Isometric added.
The company said that the new service covers all six current sectors under CBAM, including cement, iron and steel, aluminum, fertilizers, hydrogen, and electricity.
Lukas May, Chief Commercial Officer, Isometric, said:
“Exporters are going into their first CBAM verification with very little guidance on what a good submission looks like, and no way of knowing how long the process will take. The best way to avoid repeating it is to get the monitoring plan and emissions report right before they reach the verifier.”
The launch of the new service follows Isometric’s Series A financing round, with the company raising $50 million, as it moves to extend its AI-powered certification platform from its initial focus on carbon markets to the broader industrial economy, including areas such as industrial emissions, energy, fuels, and materials.

articles.summary: D’après la Maison Blanche, l’opération avait été négociée par Melania Trump. Volodymyr Zelensky lui a décerné, mercredi, une distinction honorifique.
articles.full_text:
En Ukraine, beaucoup craignaient que la mission humanitaire visant à sauver les civils pris au piège dans la ville occupée d’Olechky, dans la région de Kherson, tourne au fiasco ou à une vaste opération de propagande russe. Finalement, elle a été l’un des très rares exemples de coopération réussie entre Moscou et Kiev depuis le début de l’invasion russe, en février 2022.
Contre toute attente, la trêve locale conclue entre mardi 27 octobre et dimanche 1er novembre a été respectée, afin de permettre l’acheminement de nourriture et de médicaments, ainsi que l’évacuation d’environ 750 personnes sur les quelque 2 000 qui vivaient encore dans cette ville située sur la ligne de front. Vingt-cinq bus avaient été mobilisés. Selon des sources ukrainiennes et internationales, un quart des personnes évacuées ont choisi d’aller en Russie, tandis que les trois quarts restants ont embarqué à destination de l’Ukraine. Les autres ont préféré rester à Olechky. « J’étais sur place, j’ai discuté avec eux, et ce sont eux qui ont décidé de rester », a déclaré le commissaire aux droits humains ukrainien, Dmytro Lubinets. L’Ukraine leur a acheminé une importante quantité d’aide humanitaire, a-t-il précisé.

articles.summary: Libyan Investment Authority explores reinvestment of frozen assets in France  The Libya Observer
articles.full_text:
The Libyan Investment Authority (LIA), Libya’s sovereign wealth fund, is exploring the reinvestment of cash balances frozen in France under United Nations Security Council resolutions, aiming to preserve their value, prevent erosion and maximize returns.
LIA Chairman and CEO Ali Mahmoud held a meeting in Paris on Monday with Emmanuel Chay, Deputy Director responsible for sanctions and combating financial crime at the French Ministry of Economy and Finance, along with a team from the department overseeing sanctions and frozen assets. The meeting was also attended by Mohamed Hamouda, Chargé d’Affaires at the Libyan Embassy in France.
According to a statement published by the LIA on Facebook, the meeting addressed mechanisms for implementing relevant UN Security Council resolutions governing sanctions on frozen Libyan assets, including provisions that would allow the authority to reinvest frozen cash balances while keeping them subject to the asset freeze. The aim is to preserve their value, limit depreciation and maximize investment returns.
The LIA added that discussions also covered practical and technical matters related to its assets and investments in France, where it manages an investment portfolio valued at more than $1 billion, comprising deposits, financial investments and real estate assets.
The authority said the meeting, held at the headquarters of the French Treasury Directorate-General under the Ministry of Economy and Finance, was part of its ongoing efforts to protect its assets, preserve their value and strengthen their management in accordance with relevant international legal frameworks, in coordination with the competent authorities in countries where its assets are located.

The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy for the region. The ECB primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means keeping inflation at around 2%. Its primary tool for achieving this is by raising or lowering interest rates. Relatively high interest rates will usually result in a stronger Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
In extreme situations, the European Central Bank can enact a policy tool called Quantitative Easing. QE is the process by which the ECB prints Euros and uses them to buy assets – usually government or corporate bonds – from banks and other financial institutions. QE usually results in a weaker Euro. QE is a last resort when simply lowering interest rates is unlikely to achieve the objective of price stability. The ECB used it during the Great Financial Crisis in 2009-11, in 2015 when inflation remained stubbornly low, as well as during the covid pandemic.
Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse of QE. It is undertaken after QE when an economic recovery is underway and inflation starts rising. Whilst in QE the European Central Bank (ECB) purchases government and corporate bonds from financial institutions to provide them with liquidity, in QT the ECB stops buying more bonds, and stops reinvesting the principal maturing on the bonds it already holds. It is usually positive (or bullish) for the Euro.

As organizations scale out their production AI infrastructure, technology leaders are moving from localized model optimization to the more complex realities of industrial-grade deployment. For those who have spent years embedding machine learning into their core business processes, the current inflection point is defined by massive data pipelines, expanding compute clusters, and strict data governance. Scaling out requires an architectural evaluation: Can your infrastructure support exponential workload growth while simultaneously keeping your data entirely secure and compliant?
For European CIOs and engineering teams tasked with managing this operational expansion, scaling introduces a critical structural bottleneck: Where does our data live at scale, and who ultimately controls the underlying infrastructure?
In an era of intensive model training and widespread inference deployment, relying blindly on public cloud environments presents significant long-term structural risks. For organizations operating under stringent local regulations like the EU AI Act, expanding your AI footprint means managing larger volumes of proprietary intellectual property and customer data than ever before. If that scaling happens across jurisdictions that do not align with European privacy laws, your entire competitive advantage and regulatory standing could be compromised.
This clear need for scalable, autonomous infrastructure has catalyzed a major movement across the continent: Sovereign AI. At the absolute center of this infrastructure paradigm shift is the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart (HLRS) in Germany. As an elite computing institution, HLRS is serving as the operational blueprint for how European enterprises can aggressively scale out their AI implementations without sacrificing absolute data sovereignty.
The modern enterprise challenge: Innovation vs. autonomy
For years, commercial enterprises looking to train massive AI models had few choices outside the major global hyperscale cloud providers. While these platforms offered rapid scalability, they also created a complex web of dependencies. European enterprises frequently encountered architectural lock-in, unpredictable data egress fees, and the persistent compliance headache of transferring sensitive data across international borders.
For organizations in highly regulated sectors—such as automotive engineering, financial services, aerospace, and healthcare—these barriers were often insurmountable. Innovation slowed because the risk of exposing proprietary data was simply too high.
HLRS recognized this friction point early on. Rather than forcing organizations to compromise between computational horsepower and data security, the center designed an environment specifically tailored to the unique operational, cultural, and legal realities of European industry.
A deeply customer-centric approach to high-performance computing
HLRS does not view itself merely as a data center filled with flashing server racks; it operates as a specialized co-innovation partner for industrial enterprises and scientific researchers.
HLRS provides a unique collaborative bridge between academic research and commercial application. Its customer-centric model enables an industrial engineering team or a climate research group to receive tailored computational environments optimized for their specific mathematical models and workflows.
Consider the automotive industry, a cornerstone of the German economy. Designing the next generation of autonomous or electric vehicles requires running billions of simulation cycles. By leveraging the local, highly secure infrastructure at HLRS, these manufacturers can train complex AI vision models and run aerodynamic simulations knowing that their intellectual property remains fully insulated from external entities. The data stays in Germany, conforms entirely to European standards, yet benefits from processing speeds that rival supercomputing clusters around the world.
This customer-first focus democratizes access to elite computing. It allows midsize enterprises and massive multinational corporations alike to scale their AI ambitions without the fear of compromising their foundational data assets.
Engineering sovereign AI: The powerhouse ecosystem
Building a sovereign computing ecosystem capable of supporting next-generation AI workloads requires an extraordinary combination of hardware reliability, system architecture, and processing efficiency. To deliver this level of performance to its users, HLRS has cultivated deep strategic partnerships with industry-leading technology pioneers including HPE and AMD.
1. Architecting the future
AI and deep learning workloads are fundamentally different from traditional corporate computing. They require massive data pipelines to move fluidly across thousands of nodes without encountering bottlenecks. HPE brings its world-class supercomputing system architecture to the HLRS data center floor.
By utilizing HPE Cray Supercomputing platforms, HLRS can offer its users an infrastructure optimized for massive parallel processing. HPE advanced liquid-cooling technologies help maximize data center energy efficiency—a critical requirement for European organizations operating under sustainability mandates. For the HLRS customer, this translates to predictable, highly reliable performance even when training the most demanding, multibillion-parameter AI models.
2. Driving computational breakthroughs
Today’s AI workloads are incredibly compute-intensive, requiring advanced hardware capable of executing complex matrix mathematics at blinding speeds. HLRS integrates cutting-edge AMD processors and accelerators to meet these heavy operational demands.
AMD-powered infrastructure is deliberately engineered to handle both traditional high-performance computing simulations and modern AI training workloads simultaneously. Plus, AMD’s focus on energy efficiency per watt allows HLRS to maximize its computational output without exponentially increasing its environmental footprint. For end users, this means faster time-to-insight, accelerated product development cycles, and the ability to iterate on AI models at a fraction of the time.
By tightly integrating HPE system engineering with AMD processing innovation, HLRS delivers a sovereign computing alternative that matches—and often exceeds—the capabilities of non-sovereign platforms.
The strategic value for the enterprise CIO
For CIOs, the lesson of the HLRS model is clear: sovereign AI is no longer a niche regulatory preference; it is a core business strategy. Investing in sovereign architectures allows organizations to achieve three critical enterprise goals:
- Future-proof compliance: By anchoring AI development within a sovereign framework, organizations can be insulated from shifting international compliance regulations and the evolving complexities of global data laws.
- Intellectual property protection: Keeping model training local means proprietary algorithms, customer data, and trade secrets don’t feed into public or third-party AI models.
- Uncompromised performance: Selecting a dedicated infrastructure stack powered by HPE and AMD enables local data processing without sacrificing the speed or scale required to compete on a global stage.
As AI continues to mature, the organizations that build their digital strategies on a foundation of data autonomy and sovereignty will be the ones positioned to lead. HLRS stands as a powerful testament to what is possible when customer-focused design meets world-class technology infrastructure.

Whether accelerating scientific research, enabling digital engineering, or training advanced AI models, HPE and AMD focus on what matters most: faster insights, greater efficiency, and the flexibility to scale. articles.title: E.U. Bets €525 Million on a New Generation of Chip Design Companies - www.trendingtopics.eu
articles.summary: E.U. Bets €525 Million on a New Generation of Chip Design Companies  www.trendingtopics.eu
articles.full_text:
Europe wants a say in chips but is counting in small sums: The European Commission has just launched the European Chip Design Platform, which is meant to mobilize a total of €525 million in investment. Brussels hopes it will build a new generation of European chip design companies. By comparison, Nvidia alone has invested or announced about $10 billion (about €9 billion) in Europe’s A.I. scene within a single year, according to Jensen Huang, more than 17 times as much.
What the Platform Offers
Chip design is the part of the semiconductor value chain where much of the innovation happens, and it is exactly where Europe is weak. European chip design companies currently account for less than 1 percent of global revenue in this segment, according to the Commission. The new EuroCDP platform is meant to change that:
- Tools: Start-ups and small and midsize companies get access to chip design software, ready-made circuit building blocks (I.P. blocks), support and manufacturing capacity through a cloud platform. These are often the most expensive resources for young companies.
- Grants: Early-stage start-ups can get up to €100,000 for first prototypes. More advanced start-ups can apply for up to €16 million to cover the high costs of getting a chip to market.
- Support: 20 start-ups are already taking part in a program that prepares them technically and commercially for the market. Applicants can also get advice from national chip competence centers.
- Operations: The platform is run by a consortium led by the Belgian research center imec, supported by leading providers of design software and I.P.
Of the €525 million, €440 million will go out as grants and another €85 million into infrastructure, operations and the development of open-source design tools. €285 million comes from the E.U. budget and €240 million from the member states taking part in the Chips Joint Undertaking. The platform shows that Europe is ready to pursue its tech sovereignty goals through investment in its future as well as through policy and promises, said Henna Virkkunen, the Commission’s executive vice president for tech sovereignty.
The Nvidia Comparison
Next to Nvidia’s money, €525 million looks modest. Speaking in Paris, Mr. Huang said the chipmaker had deployed about $8 billion in Europe over the past year, plus $2 billion in new investments. As our analysis shows, Nvidia is now on board at almost every major European A.I. company, from Mistral and ElevenLabs to Lovable and Legora, and accounts for about 10 percent of all start-up investment in Europe in 2026.
The sums are not entirely comparable, though:
- Type of money: The E.U. mainly hands out grants that cost founders no equity. Nvidia buys stakes, gaining insight into the business models, growth and computing needs of its customers.
- Recipients: The E.U. platform specifically targets companies that design their own chips. Most of Nvidia’s money goes into A.I. models, applications and data centers, meaning companies that use Nvidia chips. Part of it also goes into listed holdings such as Nebius and into infrastructure.
- Dependence: With the Chips Act, the E.U. wants to reduce external dependencies. Nvidia’s stakes, by contrast, tie European companies even more closely to the U.S. company.
There is some overlap, however. Nvidia holds stakes in the French photonics start-up Scintil Photonics and in Spain’s iPronics, both of which develop components for A.I. data centers.
Europe’s Chip Design Scene
Europe does have chip designers; they are just small. Among the better known are SiPearl from France, which develops processors for supercomputers, the Dutch company Axelera AI with A.I. accelerators, and France’s VSORA with chips for A.I. applications. In manufacturing, by contrast, Europe is betting on large factories, such as ESMC’s plant in Dresden, in which TSMC is a partner, or Infineon, which is investing €1.1 billion in a GaN chip factory in Villach, Austria. The Commission argues that such capacity will only pay off if there is enough demand, and that much of it must come from European chip designers.
Big Goals, Little Money
There is plenty of criticism of the E.U.’s course. In 2025, the European Court of Auditors said the Chips Act needed a “reality check”: The goal of reaching 20 percent of the global market by 2030 was “very unlikely” to be met. According to the audit report, the E.U.’s share is likely to rise only from 9.8 percent in 2022 to 11.7 percent in 2030. The roughly €86 billion the Chips Act is meant to trigger is dwarfed by the budgets of the leading manufacturers.
For the Chips Act 2.0, which the Commission proposed in June, it is still unclear how much money will even be available. “In Chips Act 2, money will be scarcer, so we need to be more targeted in our investments,” Pierre Chastanet, the responsible head of unit at the Commission, told Science|Business. Frank Bösenberg of the Saxon industry association Silicon Saxony called the proposal “more a wish list than a real industrial policy.”
Philippe Notton, chief executive of the French chip designer SiPearl, recently laid out how large the gap is that the new platform is meant to close: Companies that design chips but do not manufacture them generate about half of global chip revenue. Europe’s share of that segment is less than 1 percent.

articles.title: Ukraine holds talks with US, Europe, and BlackRock on Prosperity Plan - RBC-Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukraine holds talks with US, Europe, and BlackRock on Prosperity Plan  RBC-Ukraine
articles.full_text:
Brussels held talks on Ukraine's Prosperity Plan, investment, and 2027 funding on Wednesday, November 4, according to a statement from Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine chief Rustem Umerov.
The first meeting focused on Ukraine's Prosperity Plan—a key document that will shape the country's postwar reconstruction, investment attraction, and economic development.
"We worked with representatives of the European Commission, the US, the UK, France, Germany, NATO, the World Bank, and BlackRock. On the Ukrainian side, the teams from the Ministry of Economy, Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Defense, and the President's Office were involved," Umerov said.
He noted that substantive work on the document is underway and added that the participants had already agreed on specific next steps and deadlines. Further details will be made public later.
Funding for 2027
The second meeting focused on Ukraine's 2027 funding. Representatives of the Ministry of Defense, Ministry of Finance, and the President's Office presented partners with detailed estimates for the coming year, including:
- Total amount of resources needed
- Funding gap that needs to be covered
- Possible sources of funding to meet these needs.
"We also discussed threats posed by Russia to Ukraine and all of Europe, as well as joint steps to counter them," the head of the Foreign Intelligence Service said.
New security architecture for Europe
Umerov said work with partners would continue tomorrow, with the sides focusing on security guarantees for Ukraine.
"This is about more than just the security of our country. It is also about a new security architecture for all of Europe after the war. Ukraine is an integral part of it. After all, without Ukraine's long-term security, Europe's long-term security is impossible," he stressed.
Earlier, The New York Times reported that the Trump administration was trying to persuade Ukraine to accept a peace deal with Russia that could involve territorial concessions in Donbas. In return, Washington is offering Kyiv potential economic benefits.
Umerov also warned about attempts by unidentified individuals to obtain information about Ukraine's new diplomatic initiatives and talks with international partners on ending the war.

articles.title: Canada, Ukraine and the case for a looser EU - GIS Reports
articles.summary: Canada, Ukraine and the case for a looser EU  GIS Reports
articles.full_text:
Ursula von der Leyen’s offer of associate status to Canada shows that the EU’s rigid structure can no longer keep pace with its expansion.
GIS Radio
Listen to our AI-powered podcast for comprehensive insights.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, speaking at the EU-Canada summit in Montreal in the presence of Prime Minister Mark Carney, proposed that Canada become an associate member of the European Union.
Enlargement has always been central to European integration. Its greatest success was admitting the Central European countries after they threw off Soviet domination. Other countries followed, mostly in Southeastern Europe. Only one member, the United Kingdom, has ever left. Brussels took considerable offense at London’s decision to leave, and negotiating subsequent bilateral agreements proved difficult.
Three members of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) – Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein – participate in the EU’s internal market through the European Economic Area (EEA) but remain outside the political union. The arrangement benefits both sides. A fourth EFTA member, Switzerland, chose bilateral agreements with the EU instead and is not a member of the internal market.
In 2013-2014, the EU proposed the Eastern Partnership to integrate Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine, an ambition that may have been illusory in the cases of Belarus and Azerbaijan. When the government in Kyiv refused to join this partnership, the 2014 Maidan protests erupted against pro-Russian President Viktor Yanukovych, ultimately leading to Russia’s annexation of Crimea and the war in Donbas.
Since then, the people of Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia in particular have aspired to association with the EU and, ideally, membership. When Western politicians backed the Maidan activists, hopes and expectations of swift accession rose. The war in Ukraine did not dampen those hopes. The expectation remains.
Excessive standards have already cost the EU one member and hampered healthy internal competition; applying them selectively would alienate others.
Prince Michael of Liechtenstein
Squeezed by Washington, Ottawa hedges
Canada’s traditionally excellent relations with the United States have deteriorated sharply, not least over U.S. tariffs. President Donald Trump has even advocated making Canada part of the U.S., an idea Canadians firmly reject. However, trade with the U.S. will remain central, and relations will improve in the interest of both sides.
Because of geography, the U.S. will remain Canada’s largest trading and security partner. However, Prime Minister Carney’s government wants to strengthen ties with other countries, with a particular focus on the EU. Ms. von der Leyen frequently puts forward ambitious proposals, most recently suggesting that Canada be granted associate status with the EU – a category that does not currently exist. Some European governments, notably Germany, France and Italy, expressed indignation at a proposal that had not been agreed upon internally. While Prime Minister Carney welcomed closer ties with the EU, he avoided the term “associate.”
More by GIS Founder and Chairman Prince Michael of Liechtenstein
- Europe’s power shift
- Are we heading toward a financial crisis?
- France in flames, Germany in decline, Europe in denial
Rethinking the European project
Whatever happens with Canada, enlargement remains on the agenda, with the Western Balkans on one side and Ukraine and Moldova on the other. Despite all the objections raised in the past, the EU will have no choice but to offer Ukraine fast-track access to its internal market once a ceasefire is reached and the war frozen. Because Ukraine will not be able to meet all the required standards in the short term, the EU will need to take a more pragmatic view of its own standards – a flexibility that may prove an advantage.
Brexit was driven largely by two factors: the EU’s petty insistence on unnecessary standards and a complete misjudgment by Prime Minister David Cameron’s government in London. Excessive standards have already cost the EU one member and have hampered healthy internal competition; applying them selectively would alienate others. Admitting Ukraine while passing over the Western Balkans would be a slap in the face to those countries. At that point, it would also be essential to admit Albania, Kosovo, Montenegro and North Macedonia.
The UK, too, may once again draw closer to the EU, in a form yet to be determined. Above all, the offer of associate membership to Canada shows that the EU needs to drastically rethink its old structure. Chief among the changes would be a truly free internal market, with sovereignty over most other matters returned to member states, which could pursue regional cooperation among themselves – in energy, for instance. Defense, likewise, should be handled by a separate association of willing countries, organized according to potential threats.
