articles.title: Could an EU carbon tax undo Canada’s 'alliance for the future' with Europe? - Canada's National Observer
articles.summary: Could an EU carbon tax undo Canada’s 'alliance for the future' with Europe?  Canada's National Observer
articles.full_text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen concluded their Montreal summit Friday with a joint announcement that presented a new “Alliance for the Future” as a shield against a “ruptured” world order.
Anchored by a European Investment Bank framework to co-finance critical mineral supply chains, the transatlantic partnership aims to be a "middle power" hedge against US trade hostility and counter China’s manufacturing monopolies.
Yet, beneath the geopolitical rhetoric is an immediate commercial pain point: the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism, also known as CBAM.
CBAM is designed to reinforce the EU’s climate commitments and guard against EU manufacturers being double-charged for the price of carbon on imported goods — once when the import moves into the economic zone, and again, by the EU’s own carbon pricing system.
The mechanism, being phased in across the 27-nation bloc as a charge on the carbon emitted making imported goods including steel and aluminum, also prevents commercial production from moving out of the EU to nations with weaker climate rules.
But CBAM could be problematic for Canadian manufacturers looking to sell into the EU. (See factbox below) A Global Affairs Canada memo obtained by the CBC says CBAM-linked charges could impact up to $2.8 billion in Canadian exports to Europe, particularly exposing iron, steel and aluminum producers already hit by US tariffs.
Carney told reporters after the summit that the CBAM issue “had been solved,” but he gave no further details. Sofia Ouslis, a spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office, told Canada’s National Observer in an email that Canada was “working toward common solutions on issues related to respective carbon pricing systems, and ensuring the European Union system recognizes carbon payments made in Canada."
“Such a resolution would provide certainty and unlock additional trade opportunities for workers and businesses on both sides of the Atlantic,” she said.
Not by 'political carve-outs'
Yet, if Ottawa wants to navigate Europe’s regulatory maze, analysts say that will not happen through "political carve-outs," but through reforms to Canadian law.
First, says Michael Brewster, senior director of global public affairs at climate policy consultancy PerezStrat, Canada needs to establish a formal method for converting Canada’s industrial carbon pricing into an EU equivalent.
Second, according to the Shareholder Association for Research and Education (SHARE), a sustainable investment house, Ottawa needs to remove the current pause on mandatory corporate climate disclosures.
Last year, Ottawa followed the US administration’s lead in pausing mandatory climate disclosures. The Canadian Securities Administration, the body set up to regulate Canada’s capital markets, said the stoppage was designed “to support Canadian markets and issuers as they adapt to the recent developments in the US and globally.”
But that move was an own-goal, SHARE wrote in a recent report. The vast majority of Canada’s largest trading partners now require corporate climate reporting aligned with International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) norms.
Jennifer Story, director of public and government affairs at SHARE, said that Canada’s decision to follow Washington “down a bad path in pressing the pause button” on climate disclosures created an “immediate commercial vulnerability” for Canadian exporters.
Where Canadian exporters should be experiencing a “natural competitive advantage” from Canada’s heavily hydro-powered grid, Story told CNO that by abandoning corporate climate disclosures, Canadian manufacturers are being charged by trading partners “as though they were the most carbon-intensive in the world.”
The data gap in standardized metrics for carbon accounting in Canada creates a “blow-back” tax on domestic industry, Story said, threatening to lock Canadian exporters out of transatlantic supply chains.
“The provision of climate information will not be a barrier to trade, but its absence certainly will be,” Story said. “Canada is looking to Europe and other international markets to diversify trade and attract investment, but our climate disclosure rules are moving in the opposite direction."
The trouble with carbon tariffs
Any calls in Ottawa for “special dispensation” on CBAM would run straight into ironclad international trade laws.
Under Article I of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), the World Trade Organization’s (WTO) “most favoured nation” principle bars Brussels from granting Canada preferential border relief without extending it unconditionally to all trading partners. A waiver for Canada without an objective measure of carbon equivalency would violate EU market parity rules and invite a WTO challenge, analysts said.
Nevertheless, pressure is building at home to secure just such preferential status.
Stephanie Kusie, Conservative shadow minister for international trade, said exporters face a new “carbon tariff under CBAM that poses a threat to Canadian industry that the Liberals cannot ignore.”
Citing federal economic assessments, Kusie said in a statement that “steel and aluminum are not exempt: adding new stress on industries already struggling amid unjustified US tariffs and sluggish growth.”
A 450-million consumer market
A more profitable path forward, according to analysts including PerezStrat’s Brewster, lies in CBAM’s deduction mechanism, which credits carbon prices paid in the country of origin against EU border charges.
However, as Canada’s carbon pricing system combines a federal set-up for large industrial emitters with a range of provincial regimes, EU customs authorities can’t automatically credit what Canadian producers are already paying.
But if Canada could refashion its system to be more in line with the EU’s, Brewster told CNO, it could effectively turn Canadian carbon pricing into a “market-access ramp” to 450 million European consumers.
This approach to Canada-EU market integration would also keep carbon revenues in Canada for use in decarbonization efforts, rather than sending the money to Europe, Brewster added. Aligning with European benchmarks “could create a system that incentivizes carbon policy in Canada in a manner that's fully aligned with free trade.”
That would blunt Canadian opponents of carbon pricing, Brewster said, because higher prices would help Canada reach European buyers with fewer trade barriers.
A joint work plan on conversion would also give Ottawa and the provinces a reason to raise carbon prices over time, Brewster said, because the money would “go back in the Canadian economy for reinvestment” rather than to the EU.
The price of pausing disclosures
Canada’s carbon-pricing friction with Europe is being compounded by a transparency gap at home.
Ottawa followed Washington’s lead in 2025 and put mandatory climate disclosures (MCD) on hold. The Canadian Securities Administration, the body set up to regulate Canada’s capital markets, said the pause was designed “to support Canadian markets and issuers as they adapt to the recent developments in the US and globally.”

SHARE said 80 nations, including the bulk of Canada’s 15 largest trading partners, now require corporate climate reporting aligned with International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) norms.
This carbon disclosure gap creates extraordinary commercial vulnerabilities as Canada seeks to add a $300-billion expansion in non-US exports by 2035, according to the report.
Without third-party verified emissions data, European auditors will assess Canadian companies “at the lowest common denominator for their sector,” treating them all as high emitters whatever their carbon footprint.
“So there's a real financial penalty,” Story said.
SHARE calculated individual institutional investors are now facing US$1.37 million a year in data collection costs linked to climate. “The provision of climate information will not be a barrier to trade, but its absence certainly will be,” Story said. “Canada is looking to Europe and other international markets to diversify trade and attract investment, but our climate disclosure rules are moving in the opposite direction."

A lasting transatlantic alliance requires Canada to move beyond its historical role as an exporter of raw materials, say observers.
EU imports of Canadian critical raw materials rose 62 per cent last year to €3.3 billion ($5.2 billion). Ollie Sheldrick, policy director at the think tank Clean Energy Canada, agrees Canada can’t let resource extraction “be the only shape of relationship that we provide,” alluding to the old description of Canadians as "hewers of wood, drawers of water.”
“We need a long-term partnership where we benefit across the supply chain,” he said.

articles.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports - BBC
articles.summary: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports  BBC
articles.full_text:
The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.
The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.
Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.
The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.
As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.
Speaking during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, the prime minister said a UK-EU deal could add up to 0.4% extra on GDP.
The deal could have the following impact:
- Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume
- It should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to
- It should also end the need for £25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases
- Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed
- It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU
In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment".
Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July.
Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his.
At Chogm on Tuesday, Burnham said: "I think people in Britain would expect me to take that with both hands, given where we've been in recent times, and that's what I'm doing."
Pressed on whether it would be acceptable for the UK to have its rules on food trade made by the EU, he said: "We're not in the EU, therefore we do have to work with them in a different way.
"But if that can get growth, if that can help our farmers, if that can remove red tape from British businesses, I think most people would expect me to go to that summit and negotiate the best deal that I can.
"And that's what I've been doing in recent weeks, leaning in, being positive, having a really constructive relationship with our European partners and hopefully we can land a good deal for Britain in terms of growth but also I hope more collaboration on controlling immigration."
Jon Walsh, the chief executive and co-founder of Bio&Me, which makes granolas, mueslis and yoghurts, told BBC 5 Live the draft deal sounded like "really good news".
"We're just a small company but when we were trying to export our yoghurts before, every time we'd send a pallet we had to pay a vet to inspect it and that was £140, and that meant that you'd lose money... so we had to stop."
The company also had problems exporting granola and overnight oats, with some shipments being returned.
"It was so frustrating because it was the same person filling out the same form and yet half would make it through and half wouldn't," Walsh said.
"You just kind of give up because you're losing money."
In an interview with ITV, Burnham said "public opinion has changed nationally" since the 2016 Brexit vote, but added he would "not run ahead of public opinion" on the issue.
"The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit," he added.
Burnham also said he had not proposed the return of freedom of movement between the UK and EU.
Asked by the BBC about the UK's relationship with the EU, Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch said that while we should "work closely", "dynamic alignment" with the EU would be a red line and "actually take us backwards".
Liberal Democrat Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said the draft deal was a "patch, not a fix".
"The real solution is to rejoin the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU," he added.
Reform UK's business spokesman Richard Tice said: "One of the key benefits of Brexit was that Britain no longer had to adhere to ridiculous EU rules.
"Returning to any form of alignment with Europe would crush Britain's competitiveness and force us to surrender sovereignty over trade policy, putting trade deals worth hundreds of billions of pounds at risk."
While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force.
The government has already announced a European Partnerships Bill which will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax.
The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days. A discount on full foreign student fees for EU students is likely to be pushed to next year alongside a plan to reconnect electricity markets.
The BBC understands the draft agreements will also include some references to UK involvement in defence co-operation schemes, access to law enforcement databases and some reassurances over the EU's "Made in Europe" plans.
A food deal will have particular significance for Northern Ireland, radically reducing the impact of the post-Brexit Irish Sea border.
Northern Ireland's Brexit deal kept it inside the EU's single market for goods. That means food products from elsewhere in the UK require paperwork and some physical checks when arriving at NI's ports. A deal will ultimately end those requirements.
While the food trade plans have been backed by supermarkets and farmers representatives, some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised the reapplication of EU rules. The post-Brexit trade deal signed by Boris Johnson's government prioritised regulatory freedoms for the UK over avoiding new regulatory red tape, checks and delays.
But William Bain, the British Chamber of Commerce's (BCC) head of trade policy, told the BBC's Today programme that business overall thought it was a "price is worth paying" to follow common rules, as companies would benefit from "lower costs, reduced delays [and] increased market access".
At the moment, he said, the requirement for Export Health Certificates can add thousands of pounds of costs to each truck carrying goods, in addition "to the delays that people find at the ports or at the borders".
"So we get lower exports because of the delays and the massive increases in costs that have come into the supply chain."
The BCC has released a new analysis of its members' views suggesting options for a closer relationship.
The business lobby group says the current trade relationship is "failing to deliver", leaving firms "struggling with a thicket of Brexit red tape" nearly six years after the UK's exit from the bloc.

Ukraine should face only temporary restrictions on agricultural products after joining the European Union, Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi told the Euronews Enlargement Summit, warning against permanent exemptions from the bloc's single market.
"We understand the concerns of European farmers, and we are ready for an open, practical discussion. Transitional measures can be part of enlargement, but they must address specific risks. And be appropriate, and have clear review and exit conditions," Koretskyi said.
Last month, the European Commission proposed excluding some Ukrainian agricultural products, notably wheat and other grains, from the EU market even after Kyiv becomes a full member, following pressure from several member states.
"They cannot become a permanent restriction or a subset of the single market," the PM added. He noted that Ukrainian farmers will have to invest heavily to meet EU food standards while rebuilding after Russia's attacks.
Since Koretskyi became PM in July, Ukraine's accession bid has gained momentum. Kyiv has set up a joint task force with the Commission to speed up negotiations.
Ukraine has recently joined the group of four accession "frontrunners", alongside Montenegro, Albania and Moldova. The Commission will publish a roadmap for them on Wednesday, setting out the steps towards membership.
For Koretskyi, EU membership is a key reason Ukraine keeps fighting Russia for its freedom, and Kyiv joining the Union will significantly strengthen the bloc's security.
"Ukraine's accession to the EU is the heart of the government policy. It is the hope for the better future and solidarity that brings peace, security and economic recovery for Ukraine and the continent," he said.
The PM wants to open all remaining negotiating chapters this year and create the conditions to start closing several during the Lithuanian presidency in the first half of 2027.
"I realised that these are ambitious objectives. We are not asking for shortcuts. We are asking for credible, merit-based paths with clear milestones and timely decision when those milestones are met," he said.

articles.title: The European Union Deforestation Regulation’s Uneven Impact: Who Is Exposed and What Are the Costs? - Impakter
articles.summary: The European Union Deforestation Regulation’s Uneven Impact: Who Is Exposed and What Are the Costs?  Impakter
articles.full_text:
For decades, agricultural expansion has driven deforestation worldwide. According to the EUDR’s preamble, the European Union imported and consumed a third of the globally traded agricultural products associated with deforestation between 1990 and 2008, and its consumption was responsible for 10% of worldwide deforestation associated with the production of goods or services over that period. In response, the bloc adopted the EUDR to reduce its contribution to global deforestation and forest degradation.The law covers seven commodities: cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya, and wood, along with a list of derived products. To be placed on or exported from the EU market, these goods must be (i) deforestation-free, (ii) legally produced, and (iii) covered by a due diligence statement.
Although the EUDR targets EU consumption, its effects will be felt well beyond the bloc’s borders. Who is actually exposed? And who will bear the cost of compliance? Understanding what the EUDR will change means looking at several factors together: countries’ exports to the European Union, the bloc’s own import patterns, how deforestation risk is assessed, and what the regulation requires of different actors along the value chain.
The EUDR’s evolving rules and risk classification
The EUDR has evolved significantly since its adoption. Its timing, product scope, and obligations have changed repeatedly since adoption, and each change affects which goods are covered, who must carry out due diligence, and how much compliance costs. The country risk classification, which determines how closely imports from each country are checked, is also subject to periodic review.
The regulation entered into force in June 2023, but its application date has been postponed twice, most recently to December 30, 2026 (June 30, 2027, for most micro and small operators). A December 2025 amendment simplified the rules, shifting the due diligence obligation to the first operator placing a product on the EU market and introducing a simplified regime for micro and small primary operators. Most recently, the European Commission adopted Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/2102 in July 2026, amending the list of covered products to remove certain products, such as cattle hides, skins, and leather, and to add products such as soluble coffee and certain palm oil derivatives. The regulation will apply to these products from December 30, 2027.
The European Commission also published updated guidance in July 2026 to reflect the December 2025 amendments, clarifying the obligations of downstream operators and of micro and small primary operators. In its May 2026 simplification review, the European Commission stated that it does not consider it appropriate to propose further amendments to the regulation itself, although the country classification will be reviewed periodically and guidance may continue to be updated. This analysis reflects the rules as they stand at the time of writing.
Three perspectives on the EUDR’s impact
Exporters: Which countries are most economically exposed?
By size, Brazil and China are the European Union’s two largest suppliers, accounting for 14.7% and 14.4% of EUDR-covered imports respectively (see figure below). Brazil’s exports span soya, coffee, wood, and cattle, while China’s are mainly wood and rubber products. These two economies are most exposed in terms of the actual volumes of trade of covered goods.
Measured by dependence, however, the picture reverses. Both Brazil and China export large volumes of other goods, so EUDR-covered sales to the European Union account for only a small part of their total exports: about 5% for Brazil and even less for China, which does not appear among the 10 most-exposed countries (see figure below). For a group of smaller exporters, the share is far higher. EUDR-covered goods sold to the European Union account for half of São Tomé and Príncipe’s total exports, mostly cocoa and palm oil. Burundi, Côte d’Ivoire, and Cameroon each rely on EUDR-covered goods sold to the European Union for at least a quarter of their total export value. Across the most exposed countries, dependence is usually concentrated in a single commodity: coffee in Burundi, Ethiopia, Rwanda, and Uganda, and cocoa in Côte d’Ivoire, Cameroon, Ghana, and Sierra Leone.
For these countries, a high share shows that much of their export value depends on EU buyers being able to document that products are deforestation-free and legally produced. If a supply chain cannot provide that information, EU buyers may drop it, or the trade may be redirected to other markets. The measure is therefore an indicator of exposure, not an estimate of losses.
The European Union: How much of the bloc’s trade is affected?
EUDR products represent a relatively small share of EU imports from outside the EU, but there is substantial concentration in particular commodities and origins.
EUDR-covered commodities accounted for around 4.3% of the European Union’s imports in 2024, but this share is not evenly dispersed. Wood alone makes up a third (35%) of those imports, while rubber, cocoa, coffee, and soya contribute roughly 13%–14%, oil palm 8%, and cattle only 2%.
That concentration deepens at the country level. For several commodities, a single country supplies over a third of the European Union’s total imports, including cocoa from Côte d’Ivoire and coffee from Brazil. Indonesia supplies around 40% of the European Union’s oil palm products’ imports, and Brazil close to half of its soya imports (see figure below).
From the European Union’s point of view, the regulation covers a manageable share of total trade, concentrated in a few product lines. But that concentration also creates vulnerability. Because the supply of commodities like cocoa and soya depends heavily on a small number of countries, a compliance problem in just one of them could affect a large share of the European Union’s supply of that commodity, even though the commodity itself represents only a small share of total EU trade.
Operators: What does EUDR compliance cost, and who will pay?
Even if aggregate compliance costs have fallen following simplification, those costs and adjustment pressures may be unevenly distributed across operators, exporters, and producers.
The compliance burden of the EUDR depends heavily on two things: the country risk classification and what the regulation requires of actors along the value chain. Under Article 29, the European Commission assigns every country one of three tiers: low, standard, or high risk. This classification reflects the European Union’s assessment of deforestation risk under its own criteria. The figure below shows the current classification.
The classification rests primarily on quantitative criteria: the rate of net forest area loss, drawn from the United Nations (UN) Food and Agriculture Organization’s Forest Resource Assessment (FAO FRA), and the rate of expansion of agricultural land or production for the seven regulated commodities, from FAOSTAT. A country qualifies as low risk if it meets any one of three conditions: it recorded no net forest loss between 2015 and 2020, its average annual forest area loss stayed below set relative and absolute thresholds, or it showed no expansion of cropland, livestock production, or overall agricultural land linked to the regulated commodities. Countries close to these thresholds undergo a second, more qualitative review that considers factors such as the strength of a country’s forest governance and its cooperation with the European Union. The regulation requires the list to be reviewed as often as necessary in light of new evidence, and the European Commission has said it envisages a first review in 2026, following the publication of updated FAO FRA data.
The risk tier determines whether operators can use simplified due diligence. It also sets, under Article 16, the minimum share of operators that competent authorities must check: at least 1% for products from low-risk countries, 3% for standard-risk countries, and 9% for high-risk countries. Half of the 20 most exposed countries are officially rated low risk under Article 29, including São Tomé and Príncipe, Burundi, Ghana, and Rwanda. Products from these countries are eligible for simplified due diligence, although their high dependence on the European Union market means that the regulation still applies to a large share of their export value. However, several highly dependent countries are rated standard risk, including Côte d’Ivoire and Cameroon, where EUDR-covered sales to the EU account for around a quarter of total exports, as well as Ethiopia, Uganda, Sierra Leone, Honduras, and Liberia. Operators sourcing from these countries must carry out full due diligence, so these countries combine high dependence on the EU market with the full set of information requirements. None of the 20 most exposed countries are rated high risk.
A European Commission report from May 2026 estimates that businesses’ annual compliance costs will total around EUR 2.0 billion, down from an estimated EUR 8.1 billion before the simplifications, a reduction of around 75%. The report sets these costs against an estimated EUR 7 billion a year in economic benefits from avoided deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions. These costs, however, will not be evenly distributed along value chains.
The due diligence obligation falls mainly on the operator that first places a relevant product on the EU market or exports it from the EU. This distinction is important because a producer is not necessarily an operator. Producers that sell their products to intermediaries, rather than placing products on the EU market or exporting them from the European Union themselves, have no direct obligations under the regulation.

articles.summary: Ukraine plans to open all negotiation clusters with the EU by the end of the year  Бабель
articles.full_text:
Ukraine wants to open all negotiation clusters with the EU by the end of 2026, and during Lithuaniaʼs EU presidency in the first half of 2027, to preliminarily close seven negotiation chapters.
Such plans were reported by the Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky in a speech at a forum on EU enlargement organized by Euronews, reports a Babel correspondent.
According to him, Ukraine, together with the Verkhovna Rada and the European Commission, is working to accelerate the implementation of the interim criteria (IBAR  Interim benchmarks.) for the first negotiation cluster "Fundamentals". 
A joint working group has been created for this purpose. Koretsky said that he is personally involved in this work, and Ukraine wants to receive a positive assessment of the implementation of the interim criteria as early as possible in 2027.
The Prime Minister acknowledged that these goals are ambitious, but emphasized: Ukraine is not asking to reduce the requirements for accession, but wants to have a clear schedule, clear criteria, and timely EU decisions after their implementation.
Koretsky was also asked whether Ukraine would agree to temporary restrictions on access to the EU agricultural market and European support after accession. The Prime Minister replied that Ukraine understood the concerns of European farmers and was ready for dialogue.
However, transitional restrictions should relate to specific risks, be proportionate and have clear conditions for review and cancellation. They should not permanently close the way for Ukrainian farmers to the EU single market.
"Ukrainian farmers will invest significantly to meet EU standards, while rebuilding their farms after Russian attacks. Ukraine offers Europe not only competition, but also new opportunities: strengthening food security, developing the processing industry and bioenergy, and strengthening European supply chains," the Prime Minister said.
What are Ukraineʼs successes on its path to the EU?
Ukraine intensified cooperation with the EU in 2014, after the victory of the Revolution of Dignity. In the same year, the Verkhovna Rada and the European Parliament simultaneously approved the Association Agreement between Ukraine and the EU.
It entered into full force on September 1, 2017. Ukraineʼs path to membership in the European Union and NATO was enshrined in the Constitution in February 2019.
On February 28, 2022, Ukraine applied for membership in the European Union. On June 17, the European Commission recommended granting Ukraine candidate status for EU membership and set out a number of conditions that the country must meet before starting negotiations on EU membership. On June 23, EU leaders gathered in Brussels for a summit, where they granted Ukraine candidate status.
In late 2023, the European Union allowed negotiations to begin. They were formally scheduled to start in 2024, but the process was blocked by Hungary under Viktor Orban. After a change of government in Hungary, the country lifted its 17-month veto on Ukraine’s EU accession in June 2026.
However, within weeks, Hungary threatened to block Ukraine’s EU accession if Kyiv did not implement an agreement on the rights of Hungarians in Transcarpathia.
On October 12, the Verkhovna Rada adopted in two readings the law on education in the languages of national minorities and indigenous peoples, and Zelensky signed the law.
After that, on October 13, the EU Council officially opened two more negotiation clusters for Ukraine on joining the European Union — “Internal Market” and “Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth”. In total, four out of six clusters have been opened so far. The previous two were opened in June (“Fundamentals”) and July (“External Relations”).

articles.title: Kazimir Warns of Further ECB Rate Hikes as Digital Euro Plans Advance - Coin Edition
articles.summary: Kazimir Warns of Further ECB Rate Hikes as Digital Euro Plans Advance  Coin Edition
articles.full_text:
- Kazimir warns that persistent inflation could require further ECB interest rate hikes.
- Rising energy and food prices, alongside a weaker euro, could increase inflationary pressure.
- The ECB plans to launch a 12-month digital euro pilot in the second half of 2027.
Slovakia’s central bank chief Peter Kazimir warned on November 2 that persistently high inflation could require the European Central Bank (ECB) to raise interest rates further, suggesting that markets may be underestimating the monetary tightening needed to bring inflation back to target.
Separately, the ECB announced on October 30 that it had selected two technology and telecommunications groups to provide network services for its digital euro project, marking another step toward testing the proposed central bank digital currency.
Kazimir Warns Inflation Could Require Further Rate Hikes
In a separate statement on November 2, Slovakia’s central bank chief Peter Kazimir warned that the ECB’s recent decision to hold interest rates steady should not be viewed as the end of monetary tightening. He cited persistent energy price pressures, rising food prices, and a weaker exchange rate that makes imports more expensive.
Kazimir said rising costs could eventually spread through the economy as businesses pass higher expenses on to consumers. He also warned that inflation expectations could shift before broader price pressures become visible in official data.
The ECB’s next policy decision is expected in December, when policymakers will have access to updated forecasts and additional economic information. Kazimir did not specify the number or size of any potential rate increases. However, he said markets might be underestimating how much further tightening would be needed to bring inflation back to the ECB’s target and keep it there.
For financial markets, the comments signal that interest-rate expectations could change if inflation remains persistent. However, the digital euro project and monetary policy decisions follow separate processes. Progress on the digital euro’s legislation and infrastructure should therefore be monitored independently of developments that could influence the ECB’s interest-rate decisions.
ECB Selects Two Digital Euro Network Groups
The ECB announced on October 30 that it had selected two groups to provide network services for the digital euro project.
The first group involves Nexi Payments and Deutsche Telekom Business Solutions. Their contract entered into force on September 28 and will initially provide connectivity for the digital euro pilot. The second group consists of Telefónica and Indra’s technology arm, Minsait. Its contract will start in May 2027.
The ECB’s official announcement states that both groups will connect participating payment service providers and national central banks to the digital euro service platform and enable communication between its components.
Both network providers will be ready as of 2029 to provide connectivity services for a potential digital euro issuance. Payment service providers will be able to choose either network to connect to the digital euro platform, subject to the ECB Governing Council’s decision on the project’s next phase.
Digital Euro Pilot Planned for 2027
The ECB intends to launch a 12-month pilot in the second half of 2027. Thirty-six selected payment service providers will participate in testing payments and assessing the system’s technical and operational capabilities.
However, the selection of network providers and the planned pilot do not constitute final approval for issuing the digital euro. The ECB has stated that a decision on issuance will only be made after the relevant European legislation is adopted and the Governing Council makes its decision. The pilot will help test the system and assess its readiness ahead of that decision.
The ECB is moving ahead with its digital euro preparations, while Kazimir’s warning puts the eurozone’s inflation outlook and potential rate hikes back in focus.

LONDON/BUCHAREST, Nov 3 (Reuters) - After seven strikes on cargo ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria last month, the US-led military alliance said it would deploy maritime patrol aircraft, radars and drones to bolster its eastern flank in the Black Sea.
Three days later, on October 23, another ship was struck just outside Romanian waters. And last week a Greek container ship was sunk by naval drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
Unabating attacks show how the escalating maritime war between Russia and Ukraine is expanding into a major challenge for NATO in the Black Sea that has left littoral member states such as Romania and Bulgaria exposed.
Military analysts said they had little doubt that these were Russian attacks. A naval drone seen on video of the last strike resembled a Russian variant, according to shipping security firm Ambrey.
"I think it's undeniably an escalation," said Sidharth Kaushal, a senior fellow at the London-based RUSI think-tank.
Russia denies targeting Ukraine's neighbours with drones and says that European governments are the ones escalating the war in Ukraine by supplying military aid. Russia's defence ministry did not respond to a request for comment for this article.
ANALYST SAYS RUSSIA IS TESTING RED LINES
Many of the ships hit in October were anchored near or sailing to or from a key Romanian canal used by Ukraine for exports. One was in Romanian territorial waters, while the other eight were in its or Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
Iulia Joja, director of the Black Sea programme for the Washington-based Middle East Institute think-tank, said Russia's attacks were taking into account the West's aversion to escalation.
"This is about testing these red lines, with full awareness that we will do everything possible to take the most minimal measures," Joja said, drawing a comparison with Russian drone incursions into NATO airspace in recent years.
A NATO official said Russian actions aimed at dissuading NATO allies from supporting Ukraine were a serious security threat and that the alliance's commitment to defending all its members, including those on the Black Sea, was "ironclad".
The official said there was a clear need for cost-effective counter-drone capabilities, but that the alliance had already committed to investing more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities in the next five years.
BLACK SEA IS CRUCIAL WATERWAY
For Romania, the Black Sea is a crucial waterway for trade and home to its offshore Neptun Deep project that will make it the European Union's largest gas producer next year. Neptun Deep was approached by a naval drone in August.
Bucharest has accused Russia of "systematic" strikes on civilian ships but stopped short of attributing individual attacks, citing the need for forensic evidence. Sofia has not blamed Russia, but said some of the attacks seem to benefit it.
The strikes come at a time when Washington is reassessing its military presence in Europe as it focuses on China. The US withdrew 1,000 troops from Romania last year.
"It's a moment in the transatlantic relationship that Putin likely wants to use," said a senior Romanian official. "The EU and NATO's attention is important and their forces are currently focusing towards the north and the Baltics."
While NATO has reinforced its "enhanced forward presence" for the Baltics and Poland, Joja said it had not done the same in Romania despite Bucharest's requests.
"Brussels and Washington still don't seem to have decided whether the Black Sea is fully part of the NATO commitment."
The Romanian official highlighted Romania's pressing need for surface-to-air interceptors and radar systems to counter threats.
Joja said the limited availability of cheap interceptor weapons, exacerbated by the war in Iran, was a central problem for the West.
NEARLY 400 VESSELS HIT IN PAST YEAR
The surge in strikes on Black Sea shipping has strangled a major conduit for exports of grain and oil used by Russia and Ukraine.
The two sides hit 317 merchant and other vessels in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov between May and October, a more than fourfold rise on the 74 vessels they struck in the previous half-year, according to Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey Analytics.
The tempo of attacks has fluctuated ahead of the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion in February.
Ukraine carried out 137 attacks on ships compared with 92 Russian ones in the third quarter, while in October, Russia hit 38 compared with 5 Ukrainian strikes, Ambrey said.
GRAIN EXPORTS FROM UKRAINE AND RUSSIA SLUMP
Ports have been battered and exports have shrivelled, forcing Russia and Ukraine to seek alternative export routes.
Russia exported just 0.3 million metric tons of grain in September through the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, down from 4.74 million metric tons in the same month last year, according to Russian export data seen by Reuters.
Ukraine suspended operations at its Black Sea ports in late July due to Russian attacks, prompting it to divert volumes to river ports on the Danube and onwards through Romania's Sulina Canal and southwards through Romania's section of the Black Sea.
Even with this alternative route, Ukraine's port exports of grain slumped to 0.81 million metric tons in September compared with 2.1 million in September last year, government data showed.
Further reducing these volumes remains Russia's primary goal with testing NATO as the secondary objective, said Andriy Ryzhenko, a naval analyst and former senior Ukrainian naval officer.
ZELENSKIY WARNS OF FOOD CRISIS
Last week's attack took place as the defence ministers and military chiefs of Romania, Bulgaria and fellow NATO littoral state Turkey met in Sofia to discuss the situation.
The defence minister of Turkey, which is waiting for a response from Moscow and Kyiv on a narrow maritime ceasefire proposal, used the meeting to warn Russia and Ukraine against further attacks.
Turkey controls the transit of warships through the Bosphorus and Dardanelles under the Montreux Convention.
Several countries, including Egypt, Turkey and India, have pushed for maritime ceasefires to avert fallout from the disruption of shipping at a time when global fuel and grain prices have soared.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday there was growing international interest in a limited ceasefire.
Russia has rejected the idea of a narrow maritime ceasefire that it says would provide respite to Kyiv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy has sounded the alarm.
"Everyone is talking about diesel and forgetting about grain. In a month or two, everyone will start talking about an agricultural crisis," he said last month.

articles.title: Ukraine moves closer to EU membership as Brussels hosts talks on post-war prosperity - EU Reporter
articles.summary: Ukraine moves closer to EU membership as Brussels hosts talks on post-war prosperity  EU Reporter
articles.full_text:
Ukraine has made significant progress towards European Union membership despite Russia's ongoing war, the European Commission said on Wednesday, as Brussels simultaneously hosted high-level international talks on Ukraine's post-war reconstruction and economic future.
Presenting the EU's annual Enlargement Package, the Commission confirmed that Ukraine had opened four negotiating clusters over the past year and met the conditions to open all remaining clusters.
European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos praised Kyiv's determination to pursue reforms during wartime.
"There is no other country in the world advancing towards EU membership under such difficult circumstances," Kos said, adding that the Commission expected all remaining negotiating clusters to open by the end of 2026.
She stressed that further reforms concerning the rule of law, anti-corruption measures and democratic institutions would be essential.
A senior EU official said Ukraine could meet key interim benchmarks in 2027, potentially allowing the provisional closure of negotiating chapters.
However, the official cautioned that Kyiv's objective of concluding accession negotiations by the end of 2028 remained ambitious and would require significantly faster reforms.
The Commission also highlighted enlargement's growing importance for European security.
EU High Representative Kaja Kallas described Ukraine as central to Europe's defence.
"Ukraine is Europe's first line of defense against Russia. Kyiv's battlefield experience is second to none, and it is critical for Europe's security and defense readiness," she said.
A senior EU official similarly stressed that Ukraine's military experience and defence industries could contribute substantially to Europe's security, alongside closer cooperation on cybersecurity, border management and critical infrastructure.
Brussels prosperity talks focus on Ukraine's reconstruction
Meanwhile, representatives from Ukraine, the EU, United States, France, Germany, United Kingdom, NATO and World Bank gathered in Brussels on Wednesday for talks on Ukraine's post-war reconstruction and prosperity.
The meeting, held at national security adviser level, followed earlier discussions in Miami and built on a prosperity framework developed with Ukraine and the United States.
According to the Commission, discussions focused on refining scenarios for Ukraine's post-war economic development and identifying financial instruments to support reconstruction, investment and long-term growth.
Brussels emphasised that Ukraine's EU accession reforms would be crucial to attracting private investment and sustaining international support.
The EU said it had provided €231.5 billion in assistance to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
Ahead of the meeting, Kallas called for a more balanced approach to peace negotiations, arguing that discussions had concentrated excessively on Ukrainian concessions.
"So far the negotiations has only been about what Ukraine should give away or what concessions they should make," she said.
Kallas urged European negotiators to uphold demands agreed by EU foreign ministers concerning Russia, arguing that Moscow's maximalist negotiating position needed to be counterbalanced.
The Brussels discussions also came ahead of planned US-Russia-Ukraine meetings in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November, announced by US envoy Steve Witkoff.
For Brussels, Ukraine's integration into the EU is increasingly viewed not only as an enlargement objective but also as a strategic investment in Europe's long-term security and stability.

articles.summary: UK interest rates: Bank of England expected to raise them for first time in over three years  BBCUK inflation to peak at 4.4% in 2027, according to FT survey of economists  Financial TimesMillions in UK brace to remortgage on worse deals as rate rise looms  The GuardianBank of England poised to hike rates for first time in 3 years  ReutersWill the Bank of England Raise Interest Rates to 4% This Week?  Morningstar
articles.full_text:
Interest rates expected to rise for first time in over three years
Policymakers at the Bank of England are expected to raise interest rates on Thursday in what would be the first increase to the benchmark rate for more than three years.
Most analysts are predicting an rise from 3.75% to 4% in a move that would increase the cost of borrowing for individuals and businesses, but boost savers.
The Bank rate has fallen from its 2023-24 peak of 5.25%, although the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has left the rate unchanged at its last six meetings.
Rising inflation, driven primarily by the cost of petrol and diesel, will push policymakers into an interest rate hike, analysts suggest.
The announcement will be made by the Bank at 12:00 GMT on Thursday.
Close attention will also be paid to any hints from the MPC on the future direction of interest rates.
"The decision is increasingly less about whether rates reach 4% and more about what follows after that," said Chris Cheverall, head of UK at trading platform CMC Markets.
"A quarter-point rise is already widely expected, but the Bank now has to balance inflation that is still too high against an economy where the growth outlook has weakened sharply."
The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) measure of inflation is well below its peak of a few years ago but has been heading back up and is expected to go higher.
The ongoing impact of the Iran war, primarily on the cost of energy and fuel, has filtered through to the UK inflation rate. Millions of domestic energy customers are braced for a hefty rise in prices in January.
How borrowers and savers are affected
The Bank of England last raised rates in August 2023.
Its base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what they charge their own customers for mortgages as well as the interest rate they pay on savings.
Were the Bank rate to rise, there would be an immediate impact on the 510,000 tracker mortgage-holders.
A 0.25 percentage point rise would mean a £31 increase in monthly repayments for someone with a typical tracker home loan, according to calculations by banking trade body UK Finance.
The 470,000 mortgage-holders on variable deals would need to wait for their lender's reaction to any Bank rate rise. Typically, a 0.25 percentage point rise would mean a £14 increase per month in repayments.
The picture for those on fixed deals is more nuanced.
While their monthly payments are not immediately affected by a rate change, their future deals are, and lenders have already "priced in" the expected rate rise when quoting new deals.
As of 4 November, the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate was 5.96%, while the average five-year rate stood at 5.99%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.
It means anyone rolling off a five-year deal faces a much bigger mortgage bill.
Broker L&C said that average mortgage rates offered by the 10 biggest lenders suggested some borrowers now faced paying almost £5,000 more each year in repayments on a £200,000 mortgage over 25 years than those who secured a remortgage deal in 2021.
Five years ago, the average five-year fixed remortgage rate among the 10 biggest lenders was 1.30%.
Relatively high fixed rates have prompted some people to consider choosing trackers, in the hope that the rate would be lower, even if the Bank rate rises in the coming months.
"The right choice ultimately depends on borrowers being confident they can stomach future rises. The devil is in the detail," said Rachel Springall from Moneyfacts.
The cost of some other new loans could be influenced by the Bank rate.
Savers, on the flipside, could see the interest rates offered to them improve in light of any rise in the Bank rate.
Ultimately, lenders - as well as policymakers at the Bank of England - are having to judge what may happen to the UK's economic outlook which is highly connected to changes in international events.

A cyberattack on several blood banks sought to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, authorities in France said late on Tuesday.
The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tonnes of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of euros.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said “temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels” on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma, in a statement.
“No health consequences have been identified and no blood products were lost,” it said.
The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites.
The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the statement said.
“Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised,” it said.
The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare.
France’s national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident.

articles.title: The Polar Vortex Is Collapsing in November: What It Could Mean for Your Winter - Severe Weather Europe
articles.summary: The Polar Vortex Is Collapsing in November: What It Could Mean for Your Winter  Severe Weather EuropeWhat is the Polar Vortex and how does it impact UK weather?  BBCThe polar vortex is about to go haywire  Scientific AmericanEurope could face colder weather as polar vortex weakens  The GuardianWill El Nino and the polar vortex mean more snow for UK this winter?  The Independent
articles.full_text:
The Polar Vortex is breaking down weeks ahead of schedule. Stratospheric winds are dropping to near zero and are forecast to reverse in the coming days, making this the earliest Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) on record. With no such event in the observed record, I searched climate model simulations for winters where the same thing happened during a strong El Niño.
The winters I found show a clear cold and snowy signal for parts of the United States, Canada, and Europe in December and January, while the Super El Niño is trying to push a very different pattern. Below, I look at both and see if the latest forecasts already show any trace of the SSW impacts in the atmosphere.
Polar Vortex: Winter Engine Over the North
 
The Polar Vortex is a broad winter circulation over the northern (and southern) hemispheres. You can imagine the Polar Vortex as a spinning wall over the polar regions, rising from the surface into the stratosphere (over 50 km/31 miles high), trapping the cold polar air inside.
This whole winter circulation is divided into two layers: the stratosphere (at higher altitudes) and the troposphere (at lower altitudes). A strong, stable Polar Vortex acts like a barrier, locking the coldest air over the North Pole and creating milder conditions for the United States and Europe, but it can be disrupted and release that cold.
The main disruption usually arises from a rise in pressure and temperature in the stratosphere, known as a Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) event, or from other dynamics that can originate from the lower levels.
Below is a 3D look at the Polar Vortex for today, and you can clearly see its actual structure. But unlike the example image above, you can see that this is a very disrupted Polar Vortex, because we are currently in the middle of a record-early Polar Vortex disruption, with the stratospheric wind reversal expected in the coming days.
I decided to also share the full 3D Polar Vortex forecast video below. It nicely shows the real disruption dynamics and how it deforms and splits the Polar Vortex core area in a Stratospheric Warming event.
 
The whole event is nicely seen in the forecast image below for 10mb level (30 km – 19 miles), which shows the split of the Polar Vortex into two cores. This is the forecast for Friday, when the wind reversal in the stratosphere is expected. You can also see the temperature compared to normal, with the temperatures in the stratosphere rising over +27°C (49°F) above normal for this time of year.
We usually monitor the overall progress and strength of the Polar Vortex by just looking at its wind in the stratosphere. A strong positive (westerly) wind indicates stable conditions or a strong Polar Vortex, but weak or even negative (easterly) winds indicate a complete reversal and a breakdown of the Polar Vortex.
Below is the latest analysis and forecast of the mid-stratospheric winds around the Polar Vortex. It shows a strong slowdown, well below normal, and also well below the previous record low strength for this time of year. We can see the projected wind reversal forecast for Friday, when the stratospheric winds first drop to zero, and a potential new reversal next week (still the same event).
All ECMWF and GEFS ensemble members show a wind reversal at some point, making it very likely. It also looks brief, with the winds recovering by mid-November. But what makes it very unusual is its early timing and a full reversal well before any past event, as seen in the image below that compares to past SSW events.
To summarize, we can see a rapid and significant disruption and slowdown of the stratospheric Polar Vortex, the earliest such on record by about three weeks. And this is important when we look at potential weather impacts this can bring.
What an Early SSW Does to December Weather Patterns
 
Before we look at the typical weather impacts from an early SSW event, we have to acknowledge the main global factors that can change or even deflect those impacts. We have to take this into consideration when looking for potential early winter impacts, as you will see below.
The 2026/2027 season global setup is dominated by a Super El Niño event in the Pacific Ocean and the westerly (positive) QBO winds up in the tropical stratosphere (21 km – 13 miles). The El Niño has a very strong weather grip, while the QBO plays its role in the stratosphere.
This tells us what data to look for when building early November SSW impact maps. To build these maps, I searched over thousands of simulated winters from global climate models and simulations and found 21 cases where the Polar Vortex collapsed in the same window during a strong El Niño and a westerly QBO.
I then compared them with similar global setups in which the Polar Vortex remained normal or strong, so the maps show what the early collapse itself added to the winter weather patterns. This is not a forecast for this winter, but the typical signal of an early Polar Vortex collapse which is added into the existing pattern.
Below is a look at the December data, first for pressure anomalies. This shows the pressure anomaly signal from the SSW itself, since all years have the same global setup. Over North America, we can see a low-pressure trend over the western U.S. and southwest Canada, and high pressure toward the east.
This looks like an attempt to boost the existing strong El Niño signal with an amplified westerly flow over the southern United States. The data above shows the Decembers that followed an early November SSW, revealing its early winter signal development.
The temperature signal is a different story. Here we can see a decent cold anomaly extending from western Canada into the United States. This is actually similar to what we can expect from a normal mid-winter Polar Vortex collapse. We must not forget this is still the SSW signal, not the actual weather outcome.
This year, such a signal is contradictory to a Super El Niño forcing, as the biggest warm anomaly wants to build right over western and central Canada. So the SSW signal can still be there, but suppressed and hard to see during a Super El Niño as strong as in 2026/2027.
Looking at the snowfall trends from the same dataset, we do see increased snowfall signal over the northern and eastern United States, and parts of southwestern and eastern Canada. This is again the SSW signal, not the overall anomaly. And it nicely shows why we are always so keen on following the stratospheric events, as the outcome can be very interesting.
Over Europe, the SSW signal for December shows a low-pressure anomaly towards the east and north, with a ridge over the western parts. This can be seen even in mid-winter SSW events, so the overall pressure signal is not very different from a November Polar Vortex collapse.
As expected, this pressure pattern means northerly flow into the continent, since a low-pressure system spins counter-clockwise. And we can see the SSW temperature signal for December does show below-normal temperatures across the continent.
In a normal atmosphere and in mid-winter, such a pattern can bring decent cold air into Europe, with some variations being called “Beast from the East” in some events. But this is not a forecast, just a simulated early November Polar Vortex collapse signal for December.
The snowfall signal follows this pattern, bringing above-normal snowfall to a large part of the continent, except for the north and northeast. Both over the United States and Europe, an early November Stratospheric Warming gives a positive signal for Winter weather to follow into December, but it has to survive the existing weather patterns.
These impacts of the Stratospheric Warming event can hide in the general circulation, as this is just its own signal. To oversimplify, if the Super El Niño wants to put a +5°F anomaly over Canada, and the SSW goes for -3°F, that can still end up +2°F above normal, despite the cold signal map.
We can look at the latest trends for the end of November to see if any similar patterns show up, despite the very strong El Niño event.
Late November Forecast: First Impacts From the Stratospheric Warming?
 
Below is the extended range trend for late November (week 4), which is in the range where we could start seeing some signals. But if the signal is there, it’s likely buried in the overall Super El Niño forcing: the main high-pressure area over Canada, the amplified low-pressure zone in the North Pacific, and a storm track over the southern United States.
This is a clear Super El Niño pattern and is perhaps slightly ahead of time in intensity. But it is to be expected, as we are dealing with the strongest Super El Niño in decades for 2026/2027.
The temperature trend for this period shows the warm anomalies under the high-pressure zone in Canada and the northern U.S. But we are starting to see a cooling trend over the southern half of the United States, under the active storm track.
The snowfall trends in this range show some snowfall signal for the Plains and towards the eastern United States. We see well-below-normal snowfall for the northern United States and Canada under the influence of the high-pressure area.
Over Europe, we can actually see a much more similar pattern to the post-SSW impact. A ridge over the southwest and a low-pressure zone to the northeast. We can’t say this is purely due to the stratospheric warming event, but the pattern is a good match to what we expect to see.
The temperature and snowfall forecast for the same period is much less extreme than the SSW signal in the images above. But we can still see a below-normal area towards the east, where it overlaps with a snowfall anomaly. The rest of the continent shows less snowfall than normal with above-normal temperatures.

articles.full_text:
A German automotive task force representing major manufacturers including Audi, Mercedes-Benz and Porsche has called for a fundamental revision of European Union vehicle emissions standards alongside reduced bureaucracy, warning that current regulations threaten the country's industrial competitiveness amid a deepening sector crisis.
A task force comprising executives from Germany's leading carmakers on Tuesday issued a 10-point agenda demanding urgent changes to European Union emissions regulations and lower energy prices to safeguard the automotive industry's future, according to local media reports.
Industry heavyweights unite
The panel includes representatives from Audi, Mercedes, Daimler Truck, Porsche and Bosch alongside the IG Metall union and employers' association Gesamtmetall, and last convened on Monday afternoon. State Economy Minister Nicole Hoffmeister-Kraut said companies need economically viable conditions to manage the industry's transformation. "We need decisions now that will make our location more competitive again," she told the newspaper.
Emissions flexibility demanded
The agenda calls for more flexible EU fleet emissions limits, including adjustments to carbon dioxide reduction targets and mechanisms to credit low-carbon materials and fuels. It also proposes a separate category for vehicles powered exclusively by biogenic fuels and electricity-based synthetic fuels. "Regarding the EU fleet regulation, we advocate incentives rather than strict quotas," the panel said, noting that early recognition of low-carbon materials should help manufacturers avoid penalties in passenger car and commercial vehicle sectors.
Infrastructure investment urged
The task force also urged investment in hydrogen, renewable fuel production and charging infrastructure for cars and trucks, alongside faster grid connections and streamlined approval procedures. Hoffmeister-Kraut established the panel following concerns triggered by Volkswagen Group's restructuring plans for Audi's Neckarsulm facility. Baden-Württemberg's automotive sector employs thousands and represents a cornerstone of Germany's export-driven economy.

articles.title: Les marques d’alcool s’appuient sur les réseaux sociaux pour contourner la loi Evin

articles.full_text:
Une « vision plus large » des stratégies mises en place par les vendeurs d’alcool pour faire la promotion de leurs produits sur les réseaux sociaux. Telle est l’ambition du nouveau rapport publié par Addictions France, jeudi 5 novembre, selon les mots de sa directrice de plaidoyer, Myriam Savy. Si les deux dernières éditions s’étaient surtout concentrées sur les collaborations commerciales entre les influenceurs et les marques d’alcool, une nouvelle méthodologie permet cette fois-ci d’« objectiver » plus finement la réalité du marketing alcoolier, à travers l’analyse, notamment, des contenus promotionnels mis en ligne par les marques.
Grâce à l’étude des bibliothèques publicitaires Meta, sortes d’archives de l’ensemble des réclames diffusées par un annonceur, les équipes d’Addictions France ont souhaité démontrer à quel point les alcooliers exploitent les « possibilités permises par les plateformes pour déployer un marketing attractif et esthétique qui joue avec les limites de la loi ». Ainsi, sur un échantillon de 54 publicités repérées parmi l’ensemble des contenus diffusés par vingt marques différentes, l’organisation relève que, dans plus de la moitié (52 %), le « message véhiculé » dépasse le cadre fixé par la loi Evin.

- Volodymyr Zelenskyy has awarded Melania Trump a national honour for her role in brokering a partial ceasefire that allowed the evacuation of civilians from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. “I hereby decree that the Order of Princess Olga, First Class, be awarded to Melania Trump, first lady of the United States of America,” a decree on the Ukrainian presidential website said on Wednesday. The text acknowledged her “significant personal contribution to humanitarian support for Ukraine, and for active human rights and charitable work”. Melania Trump last month announced a localised truce between Ukrainian and Russian forces to allow for residents of Oleshky – on the southern front – to leave after suffering weeks of shortages of food and medicine. She said nearly 800 people were evacuated. Ukraine this week accused Russia of taking advantage of the truce to strengthen its military position, while the Kremlin said adjusting positions during a ceasefire was “standard practice”.
- Melania Trump is to host officials from Moscow and Kyiv at the White House on Thursday, ahead of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending the Ukraine war. Moscow’s adviser for international economic cooperation, Kirill Dmitriev, and human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova planned to meet Trump on Thursday, provided that “all logistical arrangements work out”, Russia’s state-owned Tass news agency said on Wednesday, citing a Kremlin spokesperson. Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, said he would also be meeting Trump in Washington.
- Ukraine’s security services announced the dismissal of two senior officials linked to a high-level anti-corruption probe into bogus call centres. The head of the SBU, Oleksandr Poklad, “removed from their posts two senior SBU officials implicated in an investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau” (Nabu), the service said on Telegram on Wednesday. The SBU – Ukraine’s internal security service – said it was “providing full support” for the probe and that Poklad expected Nabu’s investigation to be “transparent, objective and impartial”. The two agencies have long been at odds. Revelations about the scam caused Ukraine’s prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko to quit in September after his offices were searched. He has denied wrongdoing.
- Zelenskyy made a surprise visit to Madrid to drum up fresh military support against Russia during a summit of Latin American leaders in Spain. He confirmed his arrival on Wednesday on social media, saying “our top priority is strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses, protecting our people and expanding defense cooperation and production”. “Further support steps are being prepared,” the Ukrainian president added, without providing detail.
- Russian attacks triggered power and water outages for hours across the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv and surrounding regions on Wednesday while Zelenskyy said the death toll from an attack in southern Ukraine had risen to 40. Multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter in the village of Komyshuvakha, near the frontline in the Zaporizhzhia region, as residents waited for humanitarian aid on Monday. In addition to those killed, Zelenskyy said 30 more people could still be buried in the rubble.
- A Ukrainian drone attack killed three members of the same family, including a child, in Russia’s border Belgorod region, officials said. The region’s general headquarters said the drone struck a minibus in which the three people, including an eight-year-old child, were travelling on Wednesday.
- The UK apologised to Ukrainian child refugees who were told to study Russian in English schools, as it launched funding for a new GCSE in Ukrainian, reports Matthew Weaver. “So many students were pushed into having to do Russian,” UK schools minister Georgia Gould said while announcing the new qualification. “I’m really sorry that they were put in that position.”
- Canada joined a coalition of countries refusing to play ice hockey teams from Russia due to the war in Ukraine, with Mark Carney saying Russian skaters will not be able to compete in the world junior championship next month.
