articles.title: China and the EU: Navigating Trade Resilience and Global Economic Stability - Alwihda Info
articles.summary: China and the EU: Navigating Trade Resilience and Global Economic Stability  Alwihda Info
articles.full_text:
Par Zhong Sheng, People's Daily
The second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism was held in Beijing on Oct. 8 and 9.
Guided by their commitment to maintaining stable and balanced trade ties as key trading partners, the two sides reviewed progress in various areas since the mechanism's first meeting, engaged in pragmatic and productive discussions, and agreed on a list of outcomes. They also issued a joint statement.
At a time when the global economic recovery faces mounting pressure and anti-globalization sentiment is gaining ground, China and the EU have demonstrated how differences can be managed and cooperation advanced through equal, professional, and constructive dialogue within the framework of World Trade Organization (WTO) rules. Their efforts have provided a valuable source of stability for an uncertain world economy.
The list of outcomes outlines 16 specific points of consensus covering trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights, and World Trade Organization (WTO) reform. These outcomes address shared concerns among industries on both sides and lay the groundwork for further cooperation.
Delegates emphasized that the meeting marks a new beginning rather than a conclusion. This statement affirms that, despite their differences, China and the EU have the wisdom and capacity to find appropriate solutions, provided they uphold mutual respect, equality, and mutual benefit while acknowledging each other's legitimate concerns.
International observers have widely welcomed the proceedings as a functional test of the consultation mechanism. By clarifying regulatory expectations and reducing uncertainty, the dialogue has helped stabilize market sentiment, delivering tangible benefits for Chinese and European enterprises alike, as well as for global economic stability.
The essence of China-EU economic and trade relations lies in mutual benefit and win-win cooperation. The current structure of bilateral trade reflects the choices both sides have made based on their respective comparative advantages, and is a natural outcome of market forces.
In 2025, trade in goods between China and the EU reached $828.11 billion, up 5.4 percent year on year, while their stock of two-way investment exceeded $280 billion. The two sides remained each other's second-largest trading partners.
Despite rising protectionist headwinds, bilateral trade in goods grew 14.2 percent year on year to $447.88 billion in the first half of 2026.
From automobiles and new energy to biomedicine and machinery, industries on both sides are deeply interconnected through supply chains and complement each other's strengths. Their markets are highly interdependent, and their shared interests are firmly established.
Reaffirming their role as key trading partners, stabilizing bilateral economic and trade ties, and promoting more balanced trade are practical steps that reflect the depth of their economic integration, and demonstrate a shared sense of responsibility to provide greater certainty for the world.
Europe has a profound tradition of free trade and has long been an important builder of an open world economy. China has noted that, in recent years, the EU has introduced a series of trade remedy measures and industrial policies whose spillover effects have attracted international attention.
Politicizing economic and trade issues, expanding the concept of national security to cover an ever-wider range of issues, and erecting unreasonable barriers to trade and investment run counter to the WTO principle of fair competition. Such measures can also disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains and ultimately undermine the upgrading and transformation of European industries themselves.
An analysis by The Economist gets to the heart of the matter: if Europe wants a thriving industrial sector, its focus should not be on keeping competitors out, but on addressing its own internal problems. Similar views echo among European business leaders, who argue that enhancing competitiveness requires addressing internal structural bottlenecks instead of limiting foreign competition.
China maintains that it has consistently partnered with Europe to overcome development challenges, rather than creating them. The principal risk to bilateral economic relations today lies not in natural trade flows, but in using "de-risking" as a justification for strategic disengagement.
China has consistently maintained that interdependence is not a risk, interconnected interests are not a threat, and openness and cooperation are the right path to shared development. China's vast market, rapidly evolving innovative applications, and complete industrial support system are indispensable to Europe's green transition and efforts to spur scientific and technological innovation.
According to the German Chamber of Commerce in China, decades of operational experience in the Chinese market have equipped German firms with competitive advantages that strengthen their global footprint.
As unilateralism and protectionist policies gain traction worldwide, the integrity of the international trading system faces mounting stress. Both China and the EU reaffirm their support for a rules-based multilateral order, endorse WTO modernization, and stress strict adherence to agreed disciplines. Aligning on these principles is vital not only for bilateral prosperity but for global economic governance at large.
Sustained dialogue and mutually beneficial cooperation remain the most effective tools for managing differences and expanding common ground.
Looking ahead, China stands prepared to work closely with the EU to address trade concerns through continuous consultation, grounded in WTO compliance and mutual respect for core interests. By deepening engagement, both sides can unlock new commercial opportunities, reinforce global supply chain resilience, and contribute to a more open, inclusive, and stable world economy.
(Zhong Sheng is a pen name often used by People's Daily to express its views on foreign policy and international affairs.)

articles.title: Eurozone Economic Growth Slows to Four-Month Low as Inflation Hits 4% - Sada Elbalad English
articles.summary: Eurozone Economic Growth Slows to Four-Month Low as Inflation Hits 4%  Sada Elbalad English
articles.full_text:
Economic activity across the eurozone slowed to its weakest pace in four months in October, as demand approached stagnation and rising energy costs intensified pressure on businesses. Business confidence also declined to a five-month low, according to a survey released on Wednesday.
The S&P Global Eurozone Composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) fell to 51.7 in October, down from 53.1 in September and below the preliminary estimate of 51.9.
Although the index remained above the 50-point threshold separating expansion from contraction, its decline signaled a loss of economic momentum at the beginning of the fourth quarter.
Chris Williamson, Chief Business Economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence said the October figures pointed to modest eurozone economic growth of approximately 0.3% at the start of the fourth quarter, following relatively strong performance in the previous quarter.
Weakening Demand and Employment Raise Concerns
The survey showed that new business orders recorded only marginal growth in October, following three consecutive months of improvement, while demand for services edged lower.
Total export orders increased for a third consecutive month, although the pace of growth slowed. Meanwhile, output expansion across both manufacturing and services weakened, highlighting the increasingly widespread slowdown across the eurozone economy.
Employment also declined slightly, as job losses in the services sector offset modest hiring gains among manufacturers.
The Eurozone Services PMI fell to 51.4 in October, compared with 53 in September, marking its lowest reading in four months.
Inflation Accelerates to 4%, Complicating ECB Policy
The slowdown in economic activity coincided with a renewed acceleration in eurozone inflation, which climbed to 4% in October from 3.8% in September, according to preliminary figures released by Eurostat on Wednesday.
The reading marked the highest inflation rate in three years and kept inflation above the European Central Bank's 2% target for an eighth consecutive month.
Higher energy prices were the primary driver, with annual energy inflation accelerating to 20.8%, its highest level since January 2023, amid rising fuel and natural gas costs linked to the US-Iran war.
Meanwhile, core inflation, which excludes food and energy, remained unchanged at 2.5%. Services inflation increased to 3.3%, while industrial goods inflation reached 1.2%, indicating that price pressures remain present across several areas of the European economy.
The latest figures present a growing challenge for the European Central Bank (ECB), which left interest rates unchanged at its most recent meeting.
Financial markets are now assessing the possibility of another rate increase in December as policymakers attempt to contain inflation without further weakening economic growth.
France Returns to Contraction as Germany and Italy Lose Momentum
Among the eurozone's largest economies, France recorded the weakest performance, with private-sector activity returning to contraction following a temporary recovery in September.
Germany, Italy, Spain, and Ireland continued to expand in October, but all four economies experienced slower growth compared with the previous month.
The latest figures follow a stronger September, when the eurozone recorded its fastest pace of economic expansion in approximately three and a half years.
That improvement had been supported by stronger demand and rising new orders, with Spain and Ireland leading growth, Germany's recovery accelerating, and France and Italy returning to expansion.
October's data, however, suggest that the European recovery is losing momentum across several major economies.
Rising Energy Costs Intensify Business Pressures
Alongside weaker economic activity, companies faced mounting cost pressures during October.
Inflation in input costs accelerated to its highest level in five months, largely driven by rising energy prices. Businesses responded by increasing the prices of their goods and services at a strong pace, although the rate of increase was slightly slower than in September.
Williamson said higher energy costs had intensified inflationary pressures during October, placing additional strain on household budgets and limiting consumer spending.
Business confidence also declined for a third consecutive month, remaining below its long-term average and signaling continued caution over the economic outlook.
ECB Faces Difficult Inflation-Growth Trade-Off
The latest economic indicators come after the ECB decided last week to keep interest rates unchanged despite persistent inflation risks.
Economists surveyed by Reuters in October had anticipated another rate increase in December, as inflation approached twice the central bank's 2% target.
Policymakers now face an increasingly difficult balancing act. Rising energy prices threaten to fuel further inflation, while weakening demand and slowing economic activity increase the risk of a broader economic slowdown.
A further tightening of monetary policy could help contain price pressures but may also weigh on business investment, household consumption, and overall economic growth.
September's Recovery Loses Strength
The eurozone economy had shown notable improvement in September, when the Composite PMI climbed to 53.1 from 52 in August, marking its strongest reading in approximately three and a half years.
The improvement reflected stronger expansion in manufacturing and services, alongside new orders rising at their fastest pace in 41 months. Export orders also returned to growth for the first time following an extended period of decline.
However, inflationary pressures were building alongside the recovery, with input costs and selling prices increasing at their fastest rates in four months amid geopolitical tensions and higher energy prices.
Outside the eurozone, separate data showed that the UK's services sector gained momentum in October. The UK Services PMI rose to 52.8 from 52.1 in September, reaching an eight-month high, supported by stronger orders and employment despite continued cost pressures.

articles.title: Bowen: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad - BBC
articles.summary: Bowen: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad  BBC'Expect the worst': What results mean for the world | Dominic Waghorn  Sky NewsWhat Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine  CNNThe Democrats will now take revenge on Trump and his ilk  The TelegraphInternational politicians react to Democrats winning US midterms  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Donald Trump deals in superlatives, so there is political karma in the sheer size of the defeat handed to him by a big majority of the voters of America.
But do not expect him to go gentle into the political twilight of his career. Losing both houses of the US Congress limits his capacity to dictate, manoeuvre and disrupt at home.
Abroad it is likely to be different.
As president of the United States and commander-in-chief of its armed forces he retains broad powers to use America's military might.
It is not easy to predict the actions and oscillations of Donald Trump. As president, he has turned policy u-turns into weapons. Some things, though, are constants.
One is his contempt for those he regards as losers, and his determination never to be seen as one.
The president might be tempted to blot out the electoral rout of the midterms by taking actions abroad. He might try to make moves that he can boast about as the decisive and victorious moves of a strong president, undiminished by an election that he insists, despite all the evidence, that was only lost because he was not on the ballot paper.
The Iran war
In the weeks leading up to the midterms the deployment of US forces and Trump's own, often belligerent, statements ramped up talk that the US was getting ready to go back to war with Iran.
On the eve of the elections, the US carried out a limited bombing raid on an Iranian island in the Gulf.
Before he was hospitalised with a stroke, the US Senator Chris Murphy, a Democrat, went to a classified briefing about potential military options for renewed war with Iran.
Without going into detail, he condemned the plans as "insane", warning that they would trigger a "devastating escalation".
There has been speculation that the Americans have plans to bomb civilian infrastructure.
Not only would that be likely to constitute a war crime, it might also be answered by devastating Iranian strikes on equivalent targets on US allies in the Gulf. Its list of potential targets could start with the United Arab Emirates, which is as close to Israel as it is to the US.
The regime in Tehran watches political developments in the US closely. It has not concealed its satisfaction that the consequences of its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have become a domestic political issue in the US.
Tehran is aware of the damage caused to Trump and the Republicans by the sustained rise in the prices of everything (from petrol and diesel to agricultural fertilisers) caused by the war and its attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
The Speaker of Iran's parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, posted a warning on social media.
He said: "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."
Benjamin Netanyahu, now acting prime minister of Israel after its election last week, and manoeuvring hard to form a new government, has repeated that he wants to bring down the Islamic regime in Tehran.
Reports in Israel and the US say that he is pushing Trump to go back to war.
Netanyahu does not have the seats to form a new government with his outgoing coalition.
But if a major war restarted and was sustained, and if Israelis came under direct fire, he could have new options of forming a unity government that he would use his considerable political skills to dominate.
War in Ukraine
The other major conflict to which Trump might turn his attention is between Ukraine and Russia, which has now lasted longer than the First World War.
Before the elections he dropped sanctions against Moscow to buy Russian diesel. He might decide to prolong and deepen sanctions relief in the hope of somehow easing the economic pressure on American consumers.
He has not been noticeably concerned about the deadly pressures on Ukrainian civilians who have been targeted by Russian ballistic missiles, now getting through in greater numbers because Ukraine's appeals for more US-made interceptors, funded by European allies, have not been answered in the way Ukraine needs and wants.
The Kremlin spokesman said Russia hoped that the election results would not impact what it called Trump's "peace-making efforts".
Donald Trump has consistently tried to force Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky into making territorial concessions to Russia to produce an agreement that would amount to capitulation for Kyiv.
Trump would add it to his improbable list of wars solved and stopped.
Smarting from electoral defeat, Trump might attempt to redouble pressure on Zelensky to accept the concessions that he has repeatedly rejected.
It is safe to say Donald Trump will continue building monuments to himself in Washington DC.
Beyond that, it is worth repeating that predictions of his next moves at home and abroad risk being wrong. But it is certain that he is not going to sit in a presidential rocking-chair and wait out his time in the White House.
Throughout his time as president, Donald Trump has relished his power and been determined to use it. That is not going to change, and there is every chance that he wants to show that if he can no longer shake America, he can shake the world.

articles.title: ITV takeover sparks fears of White House meddling in news - The Telegraph
articles.summary: ITV takeover sparks fears of White House meddling in news  The TelegraphRegulators tasked with scrutinising Sky's £1.6bn ITV deal by culture secretary  Sky NewsLisa Nandy formally intervenes in Sky’s £1.6bn ITV takeover  The IndependentSky-ITV: Lisa Nandy Says Ofcom & CMA Can Probe Competition Concerns  DeadlineUK minister formally intervenes in Sky's £1.6 billion ITV deal  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Lisa Nandy has ordered regulators to carry out a review of Sky’s £1.6bn takeover of ITV, citing concerns that the broadcaster could fall victim to interference by Donald Trump.
The Culture Secretary has told Ofcom and the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to draw up reports on the merger, which would see US-owned Sky take control of ITV’s channels and streaming service.
Ofcom will be required to consider the effect of the deal on freedom of expression and plurality of views in news media, while the CMA will review the effect on Britain’s broadcasting market.
The swoop has triggered concerns about the British broadcaster falling into foreign ownership, as well as the effect on news provision in the UK.
In a letter to Sky, Ms Nandy said both US cable giant Comcast – which owns Sky – and its subsidiary NBCUniversal were facing “ongoing political and regulatory scrutiny” in the US.
This includes an investigation launched by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), a regulator led by Brendan Carr, an ally of Mr Trump, over its agreements with local stations in the US.
The FCC launched a separate investigation last year into Comcast’s diversity policies.
Ms Nandy wrote: “There is a question over whether, in the absence of undertakings, consequences of such scrutiny in the US could affect Sky or ITV’s ability to report freely.”
Mr Trump’s assault on the media has been a hallmark of his second term, with the US president filing a $10bn (£7.4bn) defamation lawsuit against the BBC over a misleading edit of a Panorama documentary.
A judge has ruled that that Mr Trump must face questions from lawyers before the end of the year.
But the US president has reserved particular animosity for Comcast, branding Brian Roberts, the chief executive, a “disgrace to the integrity of broadcasting”.
Despite this, the US company donated $7.5m to help fund Mr Trump’s new White House ballroom.
Mr Trump’s administration has also clashed with Ofcom, claiming that Britain’s new online safety laws were harming free speech.
Alongside the public interest intervention notice (PIIN), Ms Nandy will also expand existing laws, which currently only include broadcast TV to cover on-demand programming.
The Culture Secretary, who previously said she was “minded to intervene”, has given the regulators until Jan 27 to report back, after which she will decide whether to refer the deal to a more detailed investigation.
Dame Carolyn McCall, ITV’s chief executive, previously said she expected the deal to be subject to an in-depth review lasting up to 18 months.
Sky agreed a deal in July to take control of the broadcaster behind shows including I’m a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! and Love Island.
The transaction does not include ITV’s lucrative production business, which will remain a standalone company on the London Stock Exchange.
Ms Nandy also raised concerns about the power of the combined company in its home market, which together with the BBC would hold an 86pc share of all linear news and current affairs viewing in the UK.
She warned that this duopoly could lead to an “insufficient plurality of views”, particularly if Sky and ITV were to merge their news operations.
Ms Nandy raised particular concerns about how this would affect regional news, warning that the broadcasters could face commercial incentives to cut costs by merging or closing regional newsrooms or sharing content between them.
Bosses have pledged to continue ITV’s supply deal with ITN until at least 2031, while Sky News’s independence is guaranteed until 2028 under a legally binding agreement with Comcast.
Ms Nandy said she was not aware of any evidence to suggest Comcast had previously sought to influence Sky News. However, she said this guarantee did not extend to ITV or ITN.
The Culture Secretary also raised concerns about how the merger would affect sports viewing. It is estimated that the combined company would control 60pc of all live linear sports viewing in the UK, far eclipsing the BBC.
Sky and ITV argue that the deal is necessary to give them the scale to compete with deep-pocketed rivals such as Netflix and Disney as audiences continue to move online.
They maintain that it would boost plurality by giving ITV the financial firepower to invest in journalism and compete for sports rights.
A Sky spokesman said: “We believe the transaction is in the public interest, with clear commitments already made to protect ITV’s identity, public service broadcasting obligations and the distinct editorial voices of Sky News and ITV News.”
An ITV spokesman said: “We look forward to cooperating fully with the CMA, DCMS and Ofcom in the review and will respond formally to the PIIN.”

articles.summary: Inflation Rate in the Eurozone Rises to 4.0 Percent in October  bluewin.ch
articles.full_text:
Economic Cycle
Inflation Rate in the Eurozone Rises to 4.0 Percent in October
Driven by high energy prices, inflation in the eurozone rose in October to its highest level in more than three years. Year-over-year, consumer prices rose by 4.0 percent. (File photo)
Keystone
Driven by high energy prices, inflation in the eurozone rose in October to its highest level in more than three years. Year-over-year, consumer prices rose by 4.0 percent.
Eurostat, the statistical office in Luxembourg, announced this on Wednesday following a preliminary estimate. This is the highest inflation rate since September 2023. Economists had expected this increase.
In September, the inflation rate stood at 3.8 percent, and in August, it was 3.2 percent. Inflation is thus rising at an ever-faster pace, exceeding the European Central Bank’s (ECB) medium-term target of 2 percent, at which the ECB considers price stability to be ensured.
Financial markets therefore firmly expect the ECB to raise interest rates a third time this year. The central bank will again decide on the key interest rate on December 17. The deposit rate—which is important for savers and banks—could then rise to 2.75 percent. According to the ECB’s latest forecast, people in the eurozone must brace themselves for higher inflation until at least 2027.
Bundesbank Expects Interest Rate Hike in December
Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel had spoken out in favor of a key interest rate hike as recently as Tuesday. According to the latest assessment, a rate hike is “very likely necessary,” said Nagel, who is a member of the ECB Governing Council, according to the text of his speech delivered that evening in Berlin. “From today’s perspective, (...) there is likely no way around an interest rate hike unless the inflation outlook improves significantly.”
Higher ECB benchmark interest rates are good for savers. At the same time, they make loans more expensive, which can curb demand and thus help rein in inflation. However, higher interest rates are a burden for anyone looking to invest—including businesses and homebuilders. This can slow down the economy.

articles.title: Euro zone inflation hits 4% for first time in three years as interest rate hike looms - Rich Picks Daily
articles.summary: Euro zone inflation hits 4% for first time in three years as interest rate hike looms  Rich Picks Daily
articles.full_text:
Euro zone inflation hits 4% for first time in three years as rate hike looms
A flash estimate showed euro-area inflation rising to 4% in October, the first time it has touched or surpassed that level in three years. The reading marked an uptick from 3.8% in September and aligned with economists’ expectations.
Officials attributed the increase largely to energy costs, with energy inflation rising to 20.8% from 18.9% in September. As a net energy importer, the region remains exposed to external shocks that have driven prices higher since the start of the recent conflict in the Middle East.
October’s 4% print contrasts with a prior peak of 4.3% in September 2023, underscoring the persistence of price pressures even as underlying inflation and wages are reported as broadly stable. Inflation varied across the 21 euro-area economies, with Lithuania at 6.1% and Malta at 2.3%, while all countries remained above the European Central Bank’s 2% target.
Across financial markets, the euro rose about 0.6% against the U.S. dollar on the morning following the release, aided by the broader weakness in the greenback amid ongoing U.S. midterm vote counting. The yield on the 10-year German bund, a benchmark for euro-zone debt, moved modestly higher.
The ECB held its key policy rate at 2.5% last month after delivering a 25 basis-point hike in September. Markets had been pricing in a roughly 71.8% probability of a December move before the data, with the odds rising above 72% after the release.
Policy makers continue to stress that inflation remains a central concern, even as underlying inflation and wage growth have shown resilience. The latest reading reinforces the challenge of bringing headline inflation back to the 2% target while energy prices remain volatile.
Robert Mertens, global capital markets senior analyst at Validus Risk Management, cautioned that ongoing turmoil in the French bond market is placing constraints on ECB policy. “ongoing turmoil in the French bond market is placing constraints on ECB policy,” he said.
The comment highlights how political and market dynamics could influence the ECB’s policy path even as data complicates forecasts. Analysts say the central bank can only calibrate its next moves with attention to both price developments and financial-market stability.
With the December meeting approaching, investors are weighing the likelihood of another rate increase against the risk of a more prolonged pause. The odds of a hike reflect a view that inflation remains above target and that energy-driven pressures could persist into the winter months.
In the near term, traders will monitor euro-area energy measurements, housing costs, and wage data for signs of momentum or easing. A clearer picture of the inflation trajectory could influence the ECB’s communications about the balance between policy tightening and the need to avoid excessive disruption to growth.
Market participants also expect the broader global environment to shape the ECB’s decisions. The euro’s direction will continue to respond to energy-price movements, currency dynamics, and political developments within Europe as policymakers navigate inflation and growth risks.
What’s next for policy depends on how quickly price pressures ease and whether energy costs stabilize. Officials have signaled vigilance on price developments, keeping the door open to policy adjustment if necessary to return inflation toward target.

articles.title: Sequoia shuts London office as VC firm refocuses on Silicon Valley - Financial Times
articles.summary: Sequoia shuts London office as VC firm refocuses on Silicon Valley  Financial TimesSilicon Valley investor shuts London office as US dominates AI  The TelegraphEXCLUSIVE: Sequoia Parts Ways With Half-a-Dozen Partners, Shuts European Office Amid AI-Era Reorg  Newcomer | SubstackSequoia scraps London office as UK employees face axe  City AMSequoia raises $10 billion as it dismantles parts of its global operation  CTech
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Prominent tech investor Sequoia Capital is closing its European headquarters in London in a setback to the UK’s ambitions to become a major player in the booming AI industry.
Sequoia announced the closure, which follows a similar retreat from China and India, in a social media post on Wednesday.
“We simply don’t see the need for a local presence” in Europe, the venture capital firm said. “We believe that Europe will continue to produce outlier founders and companies, and that we can continue to provide world-class support from our home base in the Bay Area.”
The international retreat marks another period of upheaval at a firm best known for lucrative bets on Apple, Google, OpenAI and SpaceX, after the tumultuous departure of former managing partner Roelof Botha a year ago.
After opening outposts in China, India and Europe over the past two decades, Sequoia has now in effect exited all overseas markets to refocus on Silicon Valley. It opened its UK office in 2020 during the pandemic-era tech boom.
Its former Chinese and Indian divisions now operate independently as HongShan and Peak XV Partners, respectively.
Sequoia’s retreat from Europe follows a similar move by its Silicon Valley neighbour Andreessen Horowitz, which closed its London office last year after less than two years. Sequoia said it would continue to invest in European start-ups from its San Francisco office.
Nevertheless the departures are a blow to Britain’s ambitions to position itself as a major player in the rapidly growing AI industry, which is dominated by the US and China.
Sequoia’s four London-based partners were given the option to relocate to the US to stay with the firm. Three of the four opted not to move, including Luciana Lixandru, who co-led Sequoia’s early-stage investment business globally. They will continue working with existing portfolio companies but will not make new investments with Sequoia.
“When given the opportunity to move to San Francisco, I chose to stay here and focus on this wonderful, imperfect ecosystem,” Lixandru said in a social media post.
Another Sequoia partner in Europe, Matt Miller, had already left the firm and launched his own fund last year.
Sequoia opened its office in London amid a broader push by US investment companies looking for new opportunities abroad. However, European technology start-ups still lag far behind their US counterparts in terms of their ability to raise capital, especially from local investors.
Despite the dominance of the US and China, London-based AI start-ups such as ElevenLabs, Ineffable Intelligence and Isomorphic Labs have still benefited from an increase in venture funding.
Sequoia’s investments in Europe have included Swedish buy-now, pay-later pioneer Klarna, German fintech Trade Republic, French accounting start-up Pennylane and German defence tech firm Stark.

articles.title: Exclusive: Top 10 largest investments by EIC in 2026 – so far - EU-Startups
articles.summary: Exclusive: Top 10 largest investments by EIC in 2026 – so far  EU-Startups
articles.full_text:
EU-Startups has received exclusive investment data directly from our partners at the European Innovation Council (EIC), revealing the ten companies that secured the largest EIC Fund commitments during the first three quarters of the year.
From quantum computing and nuclear fusion to biotechnology and space technology, the total 85 investments made by the EIC in 2026 offer a closer look at where European public investment is flowing – with the top 10 representing the forefront of European innovation.
We’ve ranked the companies by their total EIC Fund commitments signed between January and September 2026, combining multiple investments in the same company and outlining EIC contributions from larger funding rounds involving other investors. Here are the ten biggest recipients so far!
The European Champions
€34.5 million
EnduroSat (Bulgaria): Founded in 2015 by Raycho Raychev, EnduroSat is a Bulgarian SpaceTech company making satellite technology accessible and affordable. The startup designs, manufactures and operates satellites, offering a satellite-as-a-service model that allows clients to deploy space missions without developing their own spacecraft.
Its €34.5 million EIC commitment was signed on 17 August 2026. The company subsequently announced a €182 million ($205 million) funding round in September, with the EIC among its backers.
€33.3 million
Reverion (Germany): Founded in 2022 as a spin-off from the Technical University of Munich, Reverion is developing reversible power plants that can generate electricity from gases such as biogas and hydrogen, while also converting surplus electricity into storable fuels. The company is working to make renewable energy available when solar and wind production cannot meet demand. Its EIC commitments total €33.3 million across two investments signed in June and August 2026.
EU-Startups covered Reverion’s €154.2 million Series B round in September 2026, which included participation from the EIC Fund alongside Kembara, Allianz, KfW Capital and other investors.
€30 million
Pasqal (France): Founded in 2019, Paris-based Pasqal develops quantum computers powered by neutral atoms manipulated using lasers. Its technology aims to tackle complex calculations in areas such as materials science, optimisation and pharmaceutical research. The company was co-founded by a team including Alain Aspect, the 2022 Nobel Prize winner in Physics.
Pasqal secured an EIC Fund investment of almost €30 million on 30 January 2026, when it was still a privately held quantum computing scaleup. The company subsequently went public on Nasdaq in August 2026, marking a significant milestone in its growth.
Focused Energy (Germany): Founded in 2021, Darmstadt-based Focused Energy is working to turn nuclear fusion into a commercially viable electricity source. The company uses powerful lasers to compress and heat fuel, pursuing a fusion process that could eventually generate electricity without the carbon emissions associated with fossil fuels.
The German-American startup secured an EIC commitment of almost €30 million in May 2026. That same month, it announced a €213 million ($240 million) Series A, with investors including RWE, SPRIND, Prime Movers Lab and the EIC Fund. The company aims to develop a laser-fusion power plant in Biblis, Germany, during the 2030s.
€25 million
SMART Photonics (The Netherlands): Founded in 2012 and headquartered in Eindhoven, SMART Photonics manufactures photonic integrated circuits, chips that use light to transmit and process information rather than relying exclusively on electrical signals.
Its indium phosphide technology has applications in telecommunications, data centres, artificial intelligence infrastructure and sensing. The company operates as an independent manufacturer, allowing customers to develop their own chip designs without building fabrication facilities.
SMART Photonics secured €25 million from the EIC Fund in May 2026. The investment comes as the company participates in efforts to expand European photonic chip manufacturing, including a new six-inch wafer pilot line in Eindhoven.
€20 million
Leyden Labs (The Netherlands): Founded in Amsterdam in 2020, Leyden Labs is developing nasal sprays designed to protect people against respiratory viruses, including influenza and coronaviruses.
Rather than relying entirely on traditional vaccination approaches, the company’s technology delivers broadly protective antibodies directly to the respiratory tract, where many airborne infections begin. Its research aims to develop protection against multiple viral strains, including emerging variants.
Leyden Labs received an EIC commitment of almost €20 million in April 2026. EU-Startups covered its €40 million funding round in June, which brought together the EIC Fund, Invest-NL, the Gates Foundation Strategic Investment Fund, ClavystBio and other investors.
€14 million
Quandela (France): Founded in 2017 near Paris, Quandela is building quantum computers that use photons, or particles of light, to process information. The company develops both the hardware behind these machines and the software infrastructure needed to make quantum computing accessible to researchers and businesses.
Its technology combines photonic processors, single-photon sources and cloud-based computing services. In April 2026, the company reached another milestone with the inauguration of Lucy, a photonic quantum computer installed at France’s CEA computing centre.
Quandela secured an EIC Fund commitment of almost €14 million in July 2026.
€12.5 million
AURA AERO (France): Founded in 2018, Toulouse-based AURA AERO is developing lower-emission aircraft, including electric training planes and hybrid-electric regional passenger aircraft.
Its product portfolio includes the INTEGRAL family of aircraft and ERA, a proposed hybrid-electric regional airliner. The company is also developing unmanned aerial systems as it works towards expanding production in Europe and the United States.
AURA AERO received an EIC commitment of almost €12.5 million in March 2026. In April, it announced a €50 million Series B round, backed by the EIC Fund, Bpifrance’s French Tech Souveraineté fund, Safran Corporate Ventures, Innovacom and other investors.
Quobly (France): Founded in 2022 in Grenoble, Quobly is developing silicon-based quantum computers using semiconductor manufacturing techniques. A spin-off from CEA-Leti and CNRS, the startup aims to make quantum processors easier to manufacture and integrate into existing computing infrastructure.
Its approach uses silicon qubits built with industrial semiconductor processes, potentially helping quantum computing move beyond specialised research environments.
Quobly secured an EIC Fund commitment of almost €12.5 million in May 2026. EU-Startups covered its €115 million Series A round in June, led by Bpifrance, SEALSQ and STMicroelectronics, with participation from the EIC and other investors.
Proxima Fusion (Germany): Founded in 2023 as a spin-off from the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, Munich-based Proxima Fusion is developing nuclear fusion power plants using stellarators, magnetic confinement devices designed to hold extremely hot plasma in place.
The company is working towards its Alpha demonstrator, a major step in testing the technologies needed for commercial fusion energy. Its longer-term ambition is to develop power plants capable of delivering electricity at scale.
Proxima Fusion secured an EIC commitment of approximately €12.48 million in July 2026. EU-Startups covered its €411 million financing round that same month, with participation from the EIC Fund alongside investors including XTX Ventures, East X Ventures, RWE and Google.
More Information
Together, these ten companies account for approximately €224.1 million in EIC Fund investment commitments signed during the first nine months of 2026.

articles.title: Euro zone inflation rises to three-year high - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Euro zone inflation rises to three-year high  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
By Balazs Koranyi
FRANKFURT, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Euro zone inflation rose to a three-year high last month on surging food and energy costs and was set to rise further in the coming months, firming up the case for another European Central Bank rate hike in December.
Inflation in the 21 nations sharing the euro currency rose to 4.0% in October from 3.8% a month earlier, in line with expectations in a Reuters poll of economists, as energy inflation hit 20%, data from Eurostat, the EU's statistics agency, showed on Wednesday.
A more closely watched "core" figure, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, meanwhile held steady at 2.5%, in line with expectations, indicating that long-feared second-round effects have not yet materialised.
"Despite the lack of signs of second-round effects, today's inflation print adds to the already strong case for an ECB rate hike in December, as the central bank is concerned that the longer the energy shock goes on, the higher the risks of broader inflationary pressures becoming more entrenched," Nicola Nobile at Oxford Economics said.
Inflation has been climbing quickly above the ECB's 2% target this year as the US war with Iran has pushed energy costs higher, feeding through to retail prices for a bloc that imports the vast majority of its energy.
The ECB left rates unchanged last week but a long list of policymakers, including the influential heads of the German and Italian central banks, have already signalled that another move in December is now likely.
Financial markets are pricing between two and three rate hikes to the ECB's 2.5% deposit rate over the coming year, with expectations frequently shifting, in tandem with oil prices.
Sweden's central bank, meanwhile, joined peers in tightening policy on Wednesday and signalled more hikes ahead over fears energy inflation could seep into the broader economy.
The Bank of England, meeting on Thursday, is expected to follow suit, lifting its own key rate to 4.00% as it also expects inflation to exceed 4% early next year.
FOOD PRICE CONCERN
In a potentially worrisome development for the ECB, food inflation continued to accelerate with non-processed food prices rising 4.6% compared to a year earlier.
This item makes up only a small part of the consumer price basket but contains some of the most frequently bought items by households. Rapid price changes could have an oversized impact on inflation expectations, economists say.
Services inflation, the single largest item in the consumer price basket, picked up to 3.3% from 3.2% while industrial goods prices rose 1.2% after 1.1% a month earlier.

articles.title: Eurozone inflation rises to 4% in October - Financial Times
articles.summary: Eurozone inflation rises to 4% in October  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Eurozone inflation climbed to a three-year high of 4 per cent in October as surging oil and gas prices weighed on households’ spending power.
The flash estimate published by Eurostat on Wednesday was up from 3.8 per cent in September and in line with economists’ forecasts in a Reuters poll.
Annual energy inflation continued to rise to 20.8 per cent, the highest level since January 2023 and above the 18.9 per cent rate in September.
October marked the eighth month in a row that the annual inflation rate in the 21-country bloc was above the European Central Bank’s medium-term target of 2 per cent.
ECB president Christine Lagarde last week warned that a bigger and longer energy shock was “likely to drive up inflation and lower growth”. She signalled that policymakers stood ready to increase interest rates by a quarter point at their next meeting in December after keeping them on hold last week.
Annual core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, remained unchanged at 2.5 per cent, the figures released on Wednesday showed.
The closely watched figure for services inflation rose to 3.3 per cent from 3.2 per cent in September. The figure, a gauge of domestic price pressures, has remained well above the ECB’s target for more than three years.
“Energy prices were front and centre” in October’s inflation rise, said Moody’s Analytics economist Kamil Kovar, who warned that the hit would continue in the coming months, when “lower wholesale oil and diesel prices will be more than compensated by higher gas and electricity prices”.
Kovar said he expected that the ECB would raise interest rates not only in December, but also “likely in March”.
Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING, said: “Today’s inflation numbers have brought the central bank one step closer to a December rate hike.” He also pointed to “muted underlying inflationary pressure”, which he saw as an argument that “the December hike could also be the last one”.
Analysts at Pantheon Macroeconomics said an impending change of senior figures at the ECB had introduced a “wild card” for next year’s policy outlook.
If Lagarde and executive board member Isabel Schnabel were replaced by dovish candidates, the governing council could end up “erring on the side of holding fire” on raising rates beyond 2.75 per cent, they said.
The ECB has already increased borrowing costs twice since the start of the US-Iran war in February triggered a surge in oil and gas prices, raising its benchmark rate by a quarter point in June and again in September.
Worries over higher inflation and rising public debt triggered a surge in Eurozone borrowing costs in recent weeks, pushing yields of French 10-year government bonds above 5 per cent last month for the first time since 2002. They have since come back down slightly.
Stronger-than-expected economic growth could bolster the case for another rate rise. GDP across the 21-country bloc expanded by 0.4 per cent in the third quarter, twice the pace forecast by economists.
Traders have fully priced in a quarter-point increase in interest rates to 2.75 per cent by February and attribute a roughly 70 per cent chance to the ECB acting in December.
Peder Beck-Friis, economist at Pimco, said ahead of the October inflation data that he expected the ECB to lift rates next month but “the bar for going further looks high without stronger evidence that higher energy prices are generating second-round effects on core inflation”.
The euro, which had gained against the dollar since the US midterm election results, was little moved by the inflation figure. The single currency was up 0.2 per cent against the greenback by late afternoon in London, at $1.122.
Additional reporting by Ian Smith

articles.title: US midterms: Trump’s midterm rebuke could give trade partners room to resist - The Straits Times
articles.summary: US midterms: Trump’s midterm rebuke could give trade partners room to resist  The Straits Times
articles.full_text:
The drubbing for Donald Trump’s Republicans in US midterm elections could embolden some trade partners to push back against his combative policies, although they may need to tread lightly to avoid provoking him in his final two years in power.
Democrats captured majorities in both the Senate and House on Nov 3, as US voters delivered a stinging rebuke to Trump’s policies, including his tariffs, blamed alongside the Iran war for persistent inflation.
That could hand economic rival China a perceived upper hand in ongoing talks, prompt allies in Asia to slow-walk hundreds of billions of dollars in investment commitments, and give Europe more predictability over trade issues that remain unresolved.
But some partners still see choppy waters ahead, with Trump showing little sign of accepting voters’ verdict on his tariff policies that have upended global trade.
“US protectionism won’t simply disappear,” said Bernd Lange, chair of the trade committee in the European Parliament.
“A weakened Trump could become even more aggressive and unpredictable. A lame duck could quickly turn into an angry duck.”

Rajiv Bhatia, a former Indian diplomat and distinguished fellow at Gateway House think-tank, said: “A Democratic victory will not necessarily make Trump more accommodating towards any country.”
Allies hope for easier ride
Among countries that may be quietly hoping for an easier ride are America’s closest Asian allies. Japan has promised US$550 billion (S$703 billion) and South Korea $350 billion in US investments in deals intended to placate Trump.
“Democrats seem to perceive that the investment commitments were forced on allies,” said Heo Yoon, economics professor at Sogang University in Seoul, adding that countries might now feel less pressure to fulfil such commitments.
But Kazuhiro Maeshima, a professor of US politics at Sophia University in Tokyo, said the allies will not easily be able to back out. “The tariff issue is not over. If Japan’s response is slow, calls for additional tariffs could resurface,” he said.
South Korea has become a lightning rod for Trump’s anger at countries he believes have not lived up to investment pledges.
Most recently, Seoul pushed back on Trump’s assertions that it had agreed to fund Alaska LNG, a liquefied natural gas pipeline project.
Ban Kil-joo, international relations professor at Korea National Diplomatic Academy, said scrutiny from Congress over such projects could give Seoul more time to review them.
South Korea’s Foreign Ministry said it would continue to discuss economic and trade issues with the US administration, Congress and states, regardless of changes in the composition of Congress.
Trump tamed or unleashed?
In Europe, transatlantic trade tensions have largely been eased by a series of deals that have so far limited the impact of Trump’s US tariff onslaught.
But there are still potential quarrels, including whether Trump will retaliate against European countries that impose a digital services tax on US tech giants, and against a €3 billion (S$4.3 billion) loan of public money to European aircraft maker Airbus.
For India, still negotiating trade deals with the United States, the midterm results could provide an incentive to adopt a wait-and-see approach.
India’s trade minister earlier in November said the first phase of an India-US trade deal was in the final stages of drafting, but reiterated that New Delhi would proceed only if it secures an advantage over competing exporters.
No free rein with Beijing
The biggest US rival is China, which struck a trade truce with Trump that expires in January. Beijing may look for ways to use Trump’s political fragility to strengthen its hand, but also may find it harder to win him over with Congress looking over his shoulder.
“Xi Jinping will recognise that Trump’s authority has been greatly weakened by these results, and will no doubt be thinking about ways of exploiting that,” said Saul Eslake, an economist at Corinna Economic Advisory in Australia.
The US President has gone to great lengths to improve relations with Xi – including hosting him for a lavish state visit in September – and a Democratic-controlled Congress may constrain his ability to offer sweeteners for future deals.
“Democrats are unlikely to give Trump free rein on deals with Beijing,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief Asia-Pacific economist at Natixis, adding that they had already criticised Trump’s summits with Xi for limited substance on key issues like AI.
A Democratic Congress is more likely to support tighter tech export controls and scrutiny of supply chains for AI and semiconductors, which will give Trump less flexibility on concessions impacting those high-growth segments, she added.
China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters on Nov 3 that the midterms were an internal matter for the US, and that Beijing would continue to manage differences and expand cooperation with Washington. REUTERS

Andrius Kubilius says Moscow's military budget will match Europe's combined expenditure next year in purchasing power parity terms, warning that Russian military potential is not diminishing as the US pivots to the Indo-Pacific.
Berlin Security Conference
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius warned on Tuesday that Russian military spending will nearly match Europe's combined defense expenditure next year when measured in purchasing power parity terms. Speaking at the Berlin Security Conference, he stated: "Russian military potential is not diminishing." He added: "If you calculate in purchasing power parity terms, Russia is ready to spend almost the same amount that we Europeans are going to spend next year, around €500 billion ($559 billion)."
Transatlantic priorities
Kubilius stressed the need to strengthen the European pillar within NATO as Washington shifts its strategic focus toward the Indo-Pacific region. "Americans will pay more and more attention towards the Indo-Pacific region. And that is what we need to have in mind when we are talking about what capabilities we need to develop here on the European continent," he said.
He noted that Europeans must invest in addressing capability gaps to ensure continental security remains robust amid the US pivot. The commissioner emphasized that new investments should focus on areas where allies currently lack sufficient capacity.
EU-NATO relationship
The commissioner reiterated that Brussels' plans to bolster defense capabilities do not represent an alternative to the Atlantic alliance. "There really is no competition between the European Union and NATO. NATO is a military might, EU is an economic power. And our task is how to combine these two strengths into European defense capabilities which should deter Russia," Kubilius said.
The remarks come amid ongoing debates within the 32-member alliance over burden-sharing and strategic autonomy.

articles.title: European Grid Package: JPMorgan Eyes €1.2 Trillion EU Electricity Grid Investment Opportunity - Construction Review
articles.summary: European Grid Package: JPMorgan Eyes €1.2 Trillion EU Electricity Grid Investment Opportunity  Construction Review
articles.full_text:
JPMorgan Chase is positioning itself to participate in Europe’s planned €1.2 trillion (US$1.3 trillion) European Grid Package – an electricity grid modernization program, identifying the continent’s expanding power infrastructure requirements as a major opportunity for private investment.
The US banking giant is looking to expand its involvement in financing critical electricity infrastructure across Europe. This is as European governments seek to modernize ageing transmission and distribution networks, and improve energy security while accommodate growing electricity demand.
JPMorgan considers the European grid overhaul one of the region’s biggest infrastructure financing opportunities. The European Commission estimates that more than €1.2 trillion will be required to develop Europe’s electricity networks by 2040.
Daniel Rudnicki Schlumberger, who leads JPMorgan’s Security and Resiliency Initiative in Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA), said institutional investors could move quickly if European governments establish appropriate frameworks for grid operators’ revenues.
The bank’s interest also builds on its broader ambition to become a major financier of critical infrastructure. Primary attention has been to electricity networks that are increasingly important to economic competitiveness, industrial development and national security.
Ageing electricity networks create major European electricity grid infrastructure investment requirements
Europe’s electricity grid infrastructure is facing increasing pressure from the expansion of renewable energy, electrification of transport and industrial power consumption. The rapid growth of data centers is also a significant contributor to the growing power demand. This is why countries such as Germany are investing billions of euros in new gas-fired power plants and other power generating capacities in a bid to meet the rising demand.
However, insufficient transmission and distribution capacity is preventing the continent from fully utilizing its renewable energy resources. Wind and solar projects are increasingly encountering grid connection delays. This is while existing networks struggle to transport electricity from generation centers to areas of demand.
Additionally, JPMorgan estimates that approximately 500GW of renewable energy projects are waiting to connect to Europe’s electricity networks. This highlights the scale of infrastructure development required to support the continent’s energy transition.
The situation also has implications for energy security. Europe remains heavily dependent on imported energy, leaving its economies exposed to international fuel price fluctuations and geopolitical disruptions such as the long-standing Iran war.
Expanding domestic renewable generation and improving the infrastructure needed to transport electricity could help reduce this exposure. However, without sufficient grid capacity, additional renewable generation will not necessarily translate into more electricity reaching consumers.
JPMorgan explores private financing opportunities
JPMorgan’s interest in Europe’s electricity infrastructure forms part of its broader US$1.5 trillion, 10-year Security and Resiliency Initiative, announced by CEO Jamie Dimon in 2025.
The initiative is intended to support investment in strategic sectors, including energy, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing and defense.
For Europe’s electricity networks, the bank also sees opportunities to provide long-term institutional financing. This is while helping utilities and grid operators access the capital required for major infrastructure upgrades.
The financing opportunity also extends beyond large transmission projects. It will include smaller electricity distribution operators, innovative grid technologies and cross-border electricity connections.
As part of its European engagement, JPMorgan announced a grant supporting the Green Finance Institute (GFI). The grant will work on developing and piloting financing structures for these areas.
The initiative is also expected to bring together public and private sector stakeholders to explore ways of attracting additional investment into electricity networks. This will be important where smaller operators face difficulties accessing conventional financing.
EU Grids Package seeks to accelerate infrastructure development
JPMorgan’s also interest comes as the European Union works to advance reforms intended to address longstanding obstacles to electricity infrastructure development.
The proposed EU Grids Package also seeks to accelerate permitting procedures and improve cross-border electricity connections. It is also expected to address grid congestion and make better use of existing network infrastructure.
Additionally, the reforms are particularly important as the continent expands wind and solar generation. The renewables require more flexible and interconnected electricity networks to deliver power efficiently across national borders.
Investment in digital monitoring systems, battery storage and other grid-enhancing technologies could also help improve the utilization of existing infrastructure. This is while new transmission lines and substations are developed.
The financing framework will be equally important. Grid infrastructure typically requires substantial upfront capital, while generating returns over several decades. Establishing predictable regulatory arrangements could therefore help attract pension funds, insurers and other institutional investors.
JPMorgan believes that combining policy reforms with private capital will be essential to translating Europe’s electricity infrastructure ambitions into actual construction projects.
European grid modernization presents long-term construction opportunities
The anticipated €1.2 trillion European Grid Package investment represents a substantial pipeline of potential construction and engineering opportunities across Europe.
These include high-voltage transmission lines, electricity substations, distribution networks and interconnectors. Projects in battery storage facilities and digital infrastructure for managing increasingly complex electricity systems are also expected.
The expansion of cross-border transmission infrastructure will also be important in enabling countries to share electricity resources, balance intermittent renewable generation and improve regional energy security.
For construction and engineering companies, the scale of the program could create sustained demand for electrical equipment, civil engineering and grid installation.
Nevertheless, the pace at which these projects advance will depend on the ability of European governments to implement permitting reforms and establish attractive financing structures. It will also depend on the governments’ coordination of infrastructure development across national electricity markets.
With electricity demand increasing and renewable energy projects continuing to encounter connection constraints, Europe’s grid modernization program is emerging as one of the continent’s most significant long-term infrastructure development opportunities.
European Electricity Grid Modernization Program: Key Points
Location: European Union
Estimated investment: More than €1.2 trillion
Investment horizon: By 2040
Key financial institution: JPMorgan Chase
JPMorgan initiative: US$1.5 trillion Security and Resiliency Initiative
Supporting organization: Green Finance Institute
Main infrastructure: Transmission lines, substations, distribution networks, interconnectors and grid storage.
Key objectives: Grid modernization, renewable energy integration, energy security and improved electricity connectivity.
Project Stakeholders Backing the European Electricity Grid Investment
JPMorgan Chase – Prospective infrastructure financier and private capital mobilization.
European Commission – EU electricity infrastructure policy and regulatory framework.
Green Finance Institute – Development and piloting of innovative grid financing structures.

articles.title: Andy Burnham to unveil EU trade deals worth billions of pounds - The Guardian
articles.summary: Andy Burnham to unveil EU trade deals worth billions of pounds  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Andy Burnham is preparing to announce billions of pounds of trade deals with the EU covering everything from youth visas to pet passports under his vision of a much closer relationship with the bloc.
With the prime minister scheduled to meet his European counterparts in Brussels on 20 November, officials have all but agreed three deals that would allow farmers to sell freely to the continent and travellers to take their animals abroad more easily.
Although parts of the agreement will not be put in place until 2028, those close to the talks insist the process will not be derailed by disagreements on European industrial policy or UK university fees.
Elements of the deal, which will see the UK pay the EU for access to its emissions trading scheme, face criticism from those who argue Britain is signing up to the same rules it was seeking to avoid when it left the bloc.
However, Burnham said on Tuesday that the agreement would boost the UK economy by £17bn – an increase of 0.4%. His advisers believe it will also strengthen his attempts to forge much closer ties with, and even potentially rejoin, the bloc.
The prime minister told the Economist on Tuesday: “A deal could add up to 0.4% to GDP. Now that is a number that you cannot ignore.”
And he told ITV: “Public opinion has changed nationally. But I want to be really clear on this issue. I will not run ahead of public opinion. The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit.”
Burnham will meet Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, and António Costa, the president of the European Council, in Brussels later this month when the leaders are expected to announce the deals.
They include an agricultural agreement, which the government believes will be worth over £5bn to the UK economy by 2040; access to the EU’s emissions trading scheme; and a youth visa scheme for tens of thousands of people under 30.
Officials on both sides say the final text for all three deals is close to being agreed, though some key details need to be finalised. These include how many young people should be allowed to travel under the mobility scheme.
Both sides are understood to have agreed that each European member state should get its own quota under the scheme, to spread out the benefits and potential costs.
Under the proposed agricultural deal, UK companies and travellers would no longer have to get a certificate to transport live animals, including pets, into Europe. Those wanting to bring domesticated animals into the bloc would be issued with a pet passport, eradicating the need for complicated paperwork each trip.
UK producers would be allowed to continue selling some products that are banned under EU law, such as certain pesticides, for a “transition period”. Trade in other products, including live molluscs and Scottish salmon, would be freed up.
Under an agreement on emissions, the UK will pay the EU billions of pounds to avoid a cross-border carbon tax, which comes into place next January. Under a separate agreement the UK will join the EU emissions trading scheme to avoid being trapped.
And under the “youth experience scheme”, Britain and the EU would issue visas to people under the age of 30 to live, work and travel in each other’s territories. The UK is negotiating an emergency brake-style mechanism to make sure that if a member state refuses to issue its quota of visas, the UK will restrict the number of their nationals looking to travel to Britain.
Officials on both sides have now started talks over a separate joint statement setting out areas of future cooperation, including on industrial policy and tuition fees. A draft of that agreement seen by the Guardian would seek to conclude an agreement on charging European students lower fees within six months.
The Guardian revealed earlier this week that the UK was willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities for any financial loss as a result – but only if the EU agreed to grant Britain access to its protectionist Made in Europe scheme.
The draft statement, which has been prepared by the EU and not yet agreed by the UK, describes the two sides as “trusted partners” – language which the UK believes will allow it to participate in Made in Europe.
But European countries are pushing Britain to sign up to higher tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, a move UK ministers and businesses are resisting. The European draft text says both sides will “cooperate closely and explore further solutions”.
It also says the UK is likely to pay a financial contribution to the EU’s “cohesion” budget to help poorer member states – though this has not been signed off by the UK and is understood to be more likely as part of a future agreement.
The EU has also raised concerns about the UK’s plans for an accelerated programme to deport “foreign national offenders from the UK to the EU”, which it is pushing London to drop.
The agreement being announced later this month forms one half of Burnham’s attempts to reset the British conversation over Europe.

articles.title: Dolenc tells BTA the ECB may act on inflation in December - BurgasMedia
articles.summary: Dolenc tells BTA the ECB may act on inflation in December  BurgasMedia
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank (ECB) may have to take further action on inflation at its December meeting if the outlook does not improve markedly, Slovenia's central bank governor and ECB Governing Council member Primož Dolenc told BTA.
The bank has made no advance commitment to any specific decision, he said. He spoke to BTA as official monetary and financial institutions held a forum today at the Boyana Residence in Sofia.
At its meeting on 29 October, the ECB left its three key interest rates unchanged: 2.50% on the deposit facility, 2.65% on main refinancing operations and 2.90% on the marginal lending facility. It warned that rising energy prices raise the risk of higher inflation and weaker growth.
Dolenc said the ECB's main goal remains price stability, meaning inflation of 2% over the medium term. The bank's September forecasts show inflation staying high for a long time. Unresolved geopolitical conflicts keep alive the risk that prices will rise.
Dolenc's main fear is that dearer energy will slowly feed into food prices, then into other goods and services, and finally into wages.
Wages are another source of pressure. If wages and unit labour costs, which show what labour costs per unit of goods produced, rise fast, that can push prices up from within.
Weaker spending, lower investment and less borrowing could hold inflation down, Dolenc said. He said people and firms should expect prices in line with the goal of price stability.
Decisions will depend on incoming data and will be taken meeting by meeting, the governor said. There is no ready-made answer to an energy shock that fits every case. The ECB's response depends on how big and how long the shock is, and how it affects prices and the economy.
Bulgaria's first months in the eurozone are encouraging, Dolenc said. The country has used the euro since 1 January 2026.
Changing currency naturally worries people and businesses, he admitted. So far the data point to a smooth switch, similar to earlier eurozone enlargements.
Dolenc cited an analysis by ECB experts from the spring, which reached three conclusions on Bulgaria. The first is that the euro had a limited and largely one-off effect on consumer prices. Some of those price changes happened before the euro was introduced.
The second is that the currency change as a whole did not affect how people feel about inflation or what they expect on price rises. The third is that support for the euro in Bulgaria is above 50%, because initial fears of higher prices are fading. These trends match the experience of countries that joined earlier, Dolenc said.
The benefits come gradually, he said. They include deeper involvement in the single market, lower transaction costs, an end to currency risk, clearer prices and greater investor confidence.
"Adopting the euro should not be seen as the end of a process, but as the start of a new stage of economic integration," Dolenc said.
He gave Slovenia as an example. As a small, open economy, it has gained a lot from belonging to a large and stable monetary union. He said Bulgaria is well placed to do the same.
The second lesson from Slovenia is that clear explanations to people are decisive, because fears about the euro often turn out not to be fully justified. To keep public trust, he said, the country needs open information, effective consumer protection and close cooperation between institutions, business and consumer groups. The rise in support for the euro in Bulgaria shows the process is well advanced, the governor said.
Dolenc did not name a favourite to be the next country to join the eurozone after Bulgaria. He said the next enlargement depends more on political will and public support than on meeting the technical convergence criteria.
Enlargement is a complex issue with many sides, and in the end the decision is political and sovereign, guided by the Maastricht criteria and the legal and institutional framework, he said. In several EU countries outside the eurozone, public support is not strong enough now. That could change, especially in a major crisis.
Three conditions remain mandatory for joining successfully: lasting compliance with the economic criteria, structural reforms and institutions that are ready.
The planned offline payments are designed with a high level of privacy, so the information stays between payer and recipient, Dolenc explained. For online payments, data protection must be balanced with rules against money laundering and terrorism financing.
Artificial intelligence offers big opportunities for higher productivity and better banking services, but it also brings new operational and systemic risks. Dolenc said the biggest challenge for regulators is to bring under control the risks of wide and interlinked use of AI before they threaten the stability of the financial system.

articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
From the CFTC’s chair and sole commissioner Michael Selig:
Today, perpetual futures contracts on individual equity securities (the “Equity Perps”) can begin trading for the first time on CFTC-registered exchanges.
In my inaugural remarks, I directed the CFTC to use the tools at its disposal to onshore perpetual derivative products so that they can flourish in the U.S., subject to appropriate safeguards. Earlier this year, the CFTC took historic action in this regard by approving the listing of the first true bitcoin perpetual futures contract on a CFTC-regulated exchange.
Today’s announcement builds on that milestone by extending the availability of the perpetual futures contract instrument in the U.S. beyond digital commodities and into traditional securities. This expansion marks a significant step towards allowing U.S. market participants, consistent with applicable law, to avail themselves of the advantages of perpetual futures that have led to their emergence as widely sought tools for risk-management and price-discovery. I believe that bringing these types of innovative products into our regulated markets ensures that American investors and traders can access these products within the protections of the CFTC’s proven regulatory framework, rather than being forced to turn to offshore, and often unregulated, venues.
The Equity Perps were deemed approved by the Commission, pursuant to Commission Regulation 40.3, as security futures products under the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000 (the “CFMA”). The contracts are thus subject to the applicable requirements of the Commodity Exchange Act, the U.S. Federal securities laws, and the regulatory frameworks of both the CFTC and the SEC.
More than two decades ago, Congress enacted the CFMA to establish a framework for the joint regulation of security futures products. This framework recognized the complementary roles of the CFTC and SEC in overseeing American financial markets by providing a pathway for innovation at the intersection of the U.S. Federal commodity laws and the U.S. Federal securities laws. Earlier this year, and in furtherance of those principles, the CFTC and SEC entered into a historic memorandum of understanding (the “MOU”) to guide coordination and collaboration between the two agencies.
The Equity Perps build on the foundation of the CFMA and the MOU. For too long, regulatory uncertainty left innovative products, such as security futures and equity perpetual futures, stranded in what SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins has aptly described as a regulatory “no man’s land” due to a lack of harmonization between the agencies. The CFTC and SEC have turned the page on that era, and are committed to delivering regulatory clarity for innovative products and a clear path to market, rather than more casualties of jurisdictional disputes.
The Equity Perps demonstrate the strength of the ongoing commitments of the CFTC and SEC to support lawful innovation, uphold market integrity, and ensure investor and customer protection through the harmonization of the CFTC’s and SEC’s regulatory frameworks.
I would like to thank the many dedicated staff at the CFTC for their continued hard work and collaboration with the SEC. And I look forward to building on today’s milestone as the CFTC works to ensure that the new frontier of finance is built in the United States of America.
